docs.title: USD Chunks
docs.text:
usd_chunks turns a short Python module into a node in a graph, a panel of widgets, and a command you can run from the terminal. Chunks are .py files that load at runtime from the folders you point it at, in usdview or another host.

New here? The quick start takes you from nothing to a chunk on screen.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
1. Install: quick start, fixing things that don't show up, every environment variable, building the docs. In Houdini or Blender, use Houdini or Blender instead.
  2. Using the node graph: creating and connecting nodes, shortcuts.
  3. Output, View and ChunkGroup: the chunks that organise a graph instead of changing the stage.
  4. Expressions: make one param read another, like @Box.size@ * 2, and use USD's ${NAME} variables.
  5. Scripting: build a network from Python with Scene, in a script or in usdview.
  6. Chunks, params and groups: what a Chunk is, an example, and a list of params and flags.
  7. Writing a chunk: a chunk module's main(), config(), execute() and commit().
  8. Building a chunk at runtime: try an idea in the Python interpreter before making it a module.
  9. Making a chunk fast: author specs in one change block, do the maths in numpy, and what doesn't help (threads).
  10. Undo and redo: what Ctrl+Z covers (chunk edits only, by design), on which hosts, and what to use for the rest.

In short: a chunk is a Python module. main() sets up its params, execute(node) does the work, and config() holds details like its description and category.

docs.title: The graph is USD
docs.text:
usd_chunks has no file format of its own. The saved graph is plain USD:

  • A node is a prim. Each chunk is a Chunk-typed prim. Its params are inputs: attributes on the prim, and its position is stored with UsdUINodeGraphNodeAPI.
  • A wire is a USD connection. Execution order follows inputs:chunk → outputs:chunk. Passing a value from one chunk's param to another is a connection plus an expression.
  • Each chunk writes into its own layer. The layers compose into the final result.

At runtime usd_chunks also keeps a dependency graph in Python (DagNode) to know what needs to recook. It is rebuilt from the USD connections when a scene loads, so saving the stage saves the graph. What a chunk makes is ordinary USD, so a renderer, simulator or another DCC can read the result without usd_chunks installed.

docs.title: Interactive or headless
docs.text:
You write a chunk once and it runs as a panel, as a node, or from the command line with no UI at all:

usdchunks run layout.usda Transform.tx=5 -o result.usda
usdchunks run layout.usda --procedural -o network.usda

The first command flattens the result and removes the Chunk prims. The second keeps them, so the network can be opened again and re-cooked.

Procedural chunks rebuild their output when the file loads, so a saved network stores the steps, not a baked result. Chunks that write files to disk do it in a separate commit function. usdchunks run calls it once, after every chunk has cooked. See commit().

docs.title: One network, many files
docs.text:
usdchunks batch cooks a network once for each file that a glob in it matches:

usdchunks batch proxy.usda Reference.file_path='assets/*.usdc' -o 'lib/{1}/{1}.usda' --relative

The glob that matches files decides how many runs there are. The other patterns are filled from what its wildcards matched. Wildcards are used left to right, and {1} names the first match, so it can be used twice. Above, assets/fern.usdc becomes lib/fern/fern.usda. Patterns are read relative to the network's folder.

--relative writes each file's asset paths relative to it, so the library moves as one folder. A file whose result is a single root prim names it as its default prim, so a scene can reference it without a prim path.

Each run is its own usdchunks run and cooks once. --jobs sets how many run at a time. --dry-run prints the plan, including the folder the patterns were read against and every file matched, and stops there.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: usd_chunks started as a way to add tools to usdview without writing a plugInfo.json and Qt code for every one. It has grown past that: a chunk works on a USD stage, and usdview is one of several places you can run it.

docs.title: Blender
docs.text:
usd_chunks adds a USDChunks Editor node editor to Blender. You build a chunk network there, and the 3D viewport shows the result.

You need Blender 4.2 or newer. Tested with Blender 5.1 and 5.2 on Windows.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
1. Download usd_chunks_blender-<version>.zip from the Releases page. Don't unzip it.
  2. In Blender, go to Edit > Preferences > Add-ons, open the ⌄ menu at the top right, choose Install from Disk... and pick the zip.

That is all: usd_chunks and its chunks are inside the zip, and Blender has its own USD. To use your own chunks as well, set USD_CHUNK_DIRS to their folders before starting Blender.

Try it: switch any area to USDChunks Editor, click New, and press Shift+A to add a chunk.

docs.title: Install from a clone
docs.text:
To install a version that isn't released yet. Open cmd in the folder you cloned usd_chunks into:

cd C:\src\usd_chunks

The commands below are for Blender 5.2. For another version, change 5.2 in the paths.

Step 1. Install usd_chunks into Blender:

"C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.2\5.2\python\bin\python.exe" -m pip install --no-deps --upgrade --target "%APPDATA%\Blender Foundation\Blender\5.2\scripts\addons\modules" .

Step 2. Build the add-on:

mkdir dist 2>nul
"C:\Program Files\Blender Foundation\Blender 5.2\blender.exe" --command extension build --source-dir usd_chunks\frontends\blender\addon --output-dir dist

This makes dist\usd_chunks-1.0.0-rc.2.zip.

Step 3. Install the add-on: in Blender, go to Edit > Preferences > Add-ons, open the ⌄ menu at the top right, choose Install from Disk... and pick dist\usd_chunks-1.0.0-rc.2.zip.

Step 4. Try it: switch any area to USDChunks Editor, click New, and press Shift+A to add a chunk.

To join a branch into a chain, drag a node with no wires onto a wire: it goes in through a Merge, the dropped node winning, as in the other graph editors.

To open a saved network, press N in the editor, go to the USDChunks tab and click Open Chunk Network. File > Import > USD of a network file opens its network too, in a node tree of its own.

To move things in the viewport, Ctrl+click a prim to pick it, then press G, R or S to move, rotate or scale it, like a Blender object. X, Y or Z locks an axis, named as in Blender: Z is up. Click to confirm, Esc to cancel. This changes the chunk's params. A prim no chunk drives gets a Transform chunk. The handles are part of the add-on, so there is nothing else to install.

A chunk with a box handle (Blockout Box, Blocking Volume) shows a wire box when you pick its prim or select its node in the editor. Hover a face to light it, then drag it to move that face. Esc puts it back.

A network saved Y-up (usdview's default) is turned to stand up in Blender's Z-up viewport, as Blender's USD importer does, and scaled by its metersPerUnit. The file itself is not changed: chunks still read and write in the network's own space.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: Install the newer zip the same way and restart Blender; it replaces the old one. From a clone: after a git pull, run steps 1 to 3 again and restart Blender.

docs.title: Working from a checkout
docs.text:
For people working on usd_chunks itself. This links Blender to your clone, so a git pull or an edit shows up after a restart, with no reinstall.

  1. Remove the installed copies: uninstall USDChunks Editor in Preferences, and delete the usd_chunks folder from %APPDATA%\Blender Foundation\Blender\5.2\scripts\addons\modules.

  2. In cmd, run:

    mklink /J "%APPDATA%\Blender Foundation\Blender\5.2\scripts\addons\modules\usd_chunks" C:\src\usd_chunks\usd_chunks
mklink /J "%APPDATA%\Blender Foundation\Blender\5.2\extensions\user_default\usd_chunks" C:\src\usd_chunks\usd_chunks\frontends\blender\addon
setx USD_CHUNK_DIRS C:\src\usd_chunks\chunks

  3. Start Blender and turn on USDChunks Editor in Preferences.

docs.title: Other renderers in the live view
docs.text:
The live view draws with Storm, the renderer Blender ships. Another Hydra render delegate can draw it instead, if it was built against Blender's own USD: a build for any other USD won't load inside Blender.

  1. In Edit > Preferences > Add-ons > USDChunks Editor, set Hydra Delegate Folders to the delegate's folder: the one with its plugInfo.json, or with a resources folder that has it. Separate several folders with ;.
  2. In the 3D viewport, open the sidebar (N) and pick it in USDChunks > Renderer.

A launcher can set USD_CHUNKS_HYDRA_DELEGATES to the same list instead. The add-on reads it when it starts.

The live view uses the stage's RenderSettings prim: the one the stage's renderSettingsPrimPath names, or else the first one under /Render. The renderer's own settings on it, such as Aurora's aurora:max_samples or aurora:is_denoising_enabled, apply to the live view. A path tracer keeps refining the image until it is done.

docs.title: If something is wrong
docs.text:
"No module named 'usd_chunks'" when the add-on turns on. Step 1 didn't run, or used another Blender version's folder. Run step 1, then turn the add-on off and on again.

A node is red and says "Missing chunk type". The network uses a chunk that no folder on USD_CHUNK_DIRS has, such as one from your own chunk library. Its node keeps its wires and the values saved in the file. Add the folder to USD_CHUNK_DIRS and restart Blender. The USDChunks tab in the sidebar lists every missing type.

A chunk is missing from Shift+A. It needs a pip package that isn't installed. Use the chunk and Blender asks to install it. That needs Allow Online Access on, in Edit > Preferences > System > Network.

docs.title: Notes on the install
docs.text:
• Why not a plain pip install? Blender is in Program Files, which you can't write to. pip then puts the package in a per-user folder that Blender doesn't read. Step 1 installs into Blender's own add-on modules folder instead.
  • --no-deps keeps the attrs and typing-extensions Blender ships. Blender 5.2's attrs is 25.3, older than the 25.4 usd_chunks asks for, but it works.
  • --upgrade replaces the copy from an earlier install.
  • Step 1 comes before step 3. Blender turns the add-on on as soon as it's installed, and that fails if usd_chunks isn't there yet.
  • The mklink links need no admin rights. A linked usd_chunks can't find its bundled chunks by itself, so USD_CHUNK_DIRS points at them. setx only reaches programs started after it.
  • Never install usd-core or the [standalone] extra for Blender, and don't start Blender with --python-use-system-env. Blender has its own USD, and a second one in the same Blender breaks in confusing ways.

  • Other systems. To print Blender's Python and the folder for step 1:

    blender -b --python-expr "import bpy, sys; print(sys.executable); print(bpy.utils.user_resource('SCRIPTS', path='addons/modules', create=True))"

docs.title: Breakage: fracture, emit, simulate
docs.text:
Rigid bodies that break into their pieces under load, built the way Houdini builds an RBD setup: each step is a chunk that writes plain USD, the next one reads it, and the solver only solves. Nothing a step does is hidden in the solver.

Machine (Reference)  ─┐
MantleDrive (Physics Drive)
Fracture ──► Emit ──► RBD Solver ──► lights, camera, render
     output_path ─► target ─► prim_path          (param wires)

docs.title: The chain
docs.text:
Chunk Writes Houdini equivalent Fracture a PointInstancer whose prototypes are every piece of every source, with the break tree as fracture: attributes; UVs, inside/outside GeomSubsets, optional bevel Voronoi / Boolean Fracture, packed Emit on that instancer: which piece each instance is, positions, orientations, velocities, angularVelocities, primvars:rbd:emitFrame, and invisibleIds over time as a preview RBD Configure's emit, Copy to Points, Attribute Randomize on v / w Physics Drive on any part: CollisionAPI; a spinning part as a kinematic body on a RevoluteJoint with an angular velocity drive; a moving surface as velocities on its points a static / animated collider, point v on a static object RBD Solver (Breakable on) the bake: the instancer rewritten with one instance per body, per frame; spins baked onto driven parts RBD Bullet Solver

Every one of these is ordinary USD. Open the instancer after Emit and the stream is there, frame by frame; open a belt and its velocities are there. A downstream chunk wins over an upstream one on the same prim, so Emit's instances replace Fracture's laid-out ones, and the bake replaces Emit's.

docs.title: What the solver reads
docs.text:
• Bodies: the instances of its Target Prim, whose prototypes carry a fracture tree. Each starts at its positions / orientations, moving at its velocities / angularVelocities (the Initial State params stand in where those are missing), at its primvars:rbd:emitFrame (the first frame where missing). An instance still blocked when its frame comes waits a frame.

  • The world: every mesh under Collider Prims. What each one is taken as is listed in the solver's readout:

    • spinning -- a RevoluteJoint with an angular DriveAPI targetVelocity moves it, with unlimited torque; the spin is baked onto the prim;
    • animated -- its transform is time sampled; it moves with that animation's real velocity, so it drags and grips rather than teleporting;
    • moving surface -- its points carry velocities (or PhysX's surface velocity) while staying put; it carries what rests on it as far as friction allows;
    • static -- everything else.

    A part leaves the collision with UsdPhysics' physics:collisionEnabled = false -- the emitter box, typically.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text: A body breaks when the largest contact force on it within a step exceeds its strength, given in multiples of its own weight and scaling with cross-section (a piece half the size needs a quarter of the force). Its two or more children appear where it was, moving as it moved. Material is conserved: the pieces of a break tile their parent exactly.

docs.title: Not recooking
docs.text:
• Fracture uses the shared cook cache (see Caching a slow cook). The key is its params plus the source geometry. A fracture made before from the same input is read back instead of cut again, also after the scene is closed and opened.
  • RBD Solver stores each breakable bake in the same cook cache, keyed on everything that goes into it. The same input keeps its bake or reads it back. Opening a scene checks the cache once, so it comes back simulated. A new chunk downstream changes nothing upstream. Untick Cache Result to always simulate.

docs.title: Worked examples
docs.text: • cone_crusher_v2.usda -- a gyrating mantle in a conical bowl (the mantle is modelled a degree and a half off its spin axis, so spinning makes it gyrate), rock fed down a chute, gravel into a tray. The machine and the room are plain models brought in by Reference.

docs.title: Chunks, params and groups
docs.text: A Chunk holds parameters, groups and attributes. The params hold the values you change in the UI. When anything on a chunk changes, it sends a notice. Callbacks, which are plain Python functions, listen for these notices and do the work, usually writing to the stage. A callback can also add or remove params, change flags, or change what the chunk does next, all while it runs.

docs.title: A minimal example
docs.text:
A button that adds a new cube to the stage each time it's pressed:

from usd_chunks import chunk
from pxr import Usd


def addCube(owner, notice, sender):
    stage = owner.get_stage()
    count = 0
    while True:
        prim = stage.GetPrimAtPath(f"/cube{count}")
        if not prim.IsValid():
            prim = stage.DefinePrim(f"/cube{count}", "Cube")
            break
        count = count + 1


def main():
    button = chunk.Button("add_cube", "Add Cube")
    button.add_callback(addCube)

    chunk_api = chunk.Chunk("Add Cubes")
    chunk_api.add_param(button)

    return chunk_api


def config():
    return chunk.DefaultConfig(category=chunk.StandardCategory.EXAMPLES)

main() builds the chunk and its params. config() describes the module's configuration. Here it sets the category, which decides where you find the chunk in the Tab menu. Writing a chunk covers main(), config(), execute() (what the chunk does when it cooks) and commit() (writing files). See chunks/ for more examples.

docs.title: 🎛️ Params
docs.text:
Params are the parts of a chunk you interact with, like sliders, buttons and menus. Each one maps to a widget in the UI and to an inputs: attribute on the chunk's prim. A param that is still at its default value may not have the attribute yet.

Param Value Notes Slider float | int min_value, max_value, is_int=True for integers Menu str menu_items is the list of choices Checkbox bool LineEdit str Single line TextEdit str Multi-line; rows sets the height; wrap=True for prose (lines wrap, UI font) rather than code FileBrowser str | Sdf.AssetPath extensions and pattern filter the dialog ColorPicker (r, g, b) Components in the 0–1 range Button — Holds no value; use it with a callback Label str Display only, not editable Separator — Visual grouping only Custom any For a custom widget 
divisions = chunk.Slider("divisions", "Divisions", min_value=1, max_value=32, is_int=True)
mode = chunk.Menu("mode", menu_items=["linear", "smooth"])

divisions.value = 8   # read/write through .value

Use Slider rather than Spinbox for numbers. Slider handles integers with is_int=True, and it's the one the rest of the toolkit is tested with.

Param flags (ChunkFlags.ParamFlags) adjust behavior. Set one with set_flag(), clear it with unset_flag(), check it with has_flag():

output_dir = chunk.FileBrowser("output_dir", "Output Directory")
output_dir.set_flag(chunk.ChunkFlags.ParamFlags.DIRECTORY)   # pick a folder, not a file

output_dir.unset_flag(chunk.ChunkFlags.ParamFlags.LABELED)   # FileBrowser is labeled by default
output_dir.has_flag(chunk.ChunkFlags.ParamFlags.LABELED)     # False

The flags:

  • OUTPUT: a computed result. It's hidden in the UI, but other chunks can still read it as @ChunkName.param@.
  • LABELED: show a label next to the widget.
  • TRANSIENT: the value only lives in this session. It isn't saved with the scene and comes back empty when you reopen it.
  • FILE_EXISTING, DIRECTORY: for FileBrowser. Only allow existing files, or only folders. A file the chunk reads (FILE_EXISTING, or reads=True) is checked after each cook: an absolute path or a missing file logs a warning.

A relative path in a param is relative to the network file, as in USD (see "File paths" in scripting.md). Hand it to USD as chunk.anchor_file(node, value), which anchors a ./ or ../ path there. A chunk that opens the file itself, as CAD Import does, gets the file from chunk.resolve_file(node, value) instead of reading the value from the working directory. - PRIM_SELECTION, PROP_SELECTION: for LineEdit. The value is a prim or property path, so the UI lets you pick it from the selection. - PY_SYNTAX_HIGHLIGHT, USD_SYNTAX_HIGHLIGHT: syntax highlighting for TextEdit.

State (ChunkFlags.State) describes what a param is doing right now: HIDDEN, DISABLED, COLLAPSED, SELECTED and STALE. STALE means a result is out of date with its inputs. The chunk sets and clears it itself (the RBD Solver does), and the graph shows it as an amber badge on the node.

docs.title: 📁 Groups
docs.text:
Groups hold params and other groups, and give a chunk its layout. A Chunk is a group too, so add_param, add_params, get_param and get_my_params work at every level.

  • Group: a plain container.
  • ListGroup: items can be added and removed while it runs, for lists of any length.
  • Vector: a fixed set of params used as one value, like X, Y and Z. Expressions can refer to the whole vector as @Node.vecParam@.
transform = chunk.Group("transform", "Transform")
transform.add_params([
    chunk.Slider("tx", min_value=-100, max_value=100),
    chunk.Slider("ty", min_value=-100, max_value=100),
])
chunk_api.add_param(transform)

ChunkFlags.GroupFlags controls how a group looks: LABELED, COLLAPSABLE, FRAMED, LIST and CONTEXT. CONTEXT is the important one. A context group is shown as a workspace that holds other chunks, not as a node (in the Qt plugin, it's a tab). ChunkGroup uses it.

docs.title: Chunks that need pip packages
docs.text:
A chunk module can import third-party packages at its top level, as long as it declares them in config():

from usd_chunks import chunk

import numpy as np
import cv2 as cv


def show_plot(owner, notice, sender):
    """Draw a two-segment line from the chunk's three sliders."""

    def height(name):
        return int((1 - owner.get_param(name).value / 10) * 511)

    a, b, c = height("A_param"), height("B_param"), height("C_param")
    img = np.zeros((512, 512, 3), np.uint8)
    cv.line(img, (0, a), (256, b), (255, 0, 0), 5)
    cv.line(img, (256, b), (511, c), (255, 0, 0), 5)
    cv.imshow("requirements example", img)


def main():
    node = chunk.Chunk("Req")
    for name in ("A_param", "B_param", "C_param"):
        node.add_param(chunk.Slider(name, flags=chunk.ChunkFlags.ParamFlags.LABELED))
    button = chunk.Button("plot", "Plot")
    node.add_param(button)
    node.add_callback(show_plot, sender=button)
    return node


def config():
    return chunk.DefaultConfig(
        chunk.StandardCategory.EXAMPLES,
        "Plots three sliders with OpenCV.",
        requirements=["opencv-python>=4,<5", "numpy>=2,<3"],
    )

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The registry reads config() straight from the source, without running the module, so the requirements are known even when the packages are missing and import cv2 would fail.

When a chunk is loaded with packages missing, the host asks once for all of them, naming the chunk: usdview shows "OK to install requests for chunk AMDMaterialXLibrary?" with Yes/No, usdchunks run asks the same on an interactive terminal, and Blender shows a popup once the add-on has loaded (one checkbox per chunk when several need something).

  • Yes: they are installed into USD_CHUNK_DEPENDENCY_DIR (a subfolder per Python version), with pip's progress shown: a progress dialog in usdview, pip's output in the terminal, the status bar and USDChunks sidebar in Blender. That directory is on sys.path, and then the module body runs.
  • No, or nobody to ask (Blender, CI, a piped run): nothing is installed. The chunk does not load, and a warning names the missing packages and the pip command to install them. A "no" is remembered until restart, so a network with ten of that chunk asks once.

Opening someone else's network never adds packages without your yes. USD_CHUNK_AUTO_INSTALL changes the default: 1 installs without asking, 0 never installs and only warns.

docs.title: Declare a range, not a bare name
docs.text:
Write each requirement with a version range, such as numpy>=2,<3. A bare numpy still works, but you get a warning: two runs a month apart could use different libraries from the same network, and nothing recorded would explain the difference. An exact pin (==) is also discouraged, because two chunks pinning different versions of one package cannot both be satisfied.

Declare every third-party package the module imports. An undeclared import is an install that breaks on a clean machine, and a version that never reaches a run's manifest. usdchunks deps lists chunks with undeclared or unconstrained requirements, and usdchunks deps --strict fails on them, for CI.

docs.title: Output, View and ChunkGroup
docs.text: These chunks don't change the stage themselves. They control when things cook and how a graph is organised. All are in chunks/core/: output.py, view.py and chunkgroup.py.

docs.title: 🔎 At a glance
docs.text:
• Output is what a graph delivers: the end of its chain. usdchunks run cooks to it, and so does the graph whenever no View is active. Press 1 to cook to it, or right-click a chunk and choose Set Output to end the graph there.
  • View is where you look while working. Right-click a chunk and choose Set View 2 or Set View 3 to look at it.
  • ChunkGroup is a subnet. Double-click its header to go inside and build like in any other graph. Click the path at the top-left of the graph to come back out.

The rest of this page goes into more detail on each.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Each graph level (the top level, or the inside of a ChunkGroup) has one Output, wired to the end of its chain. A graph with neither an Output nor a View gets an Output added and connected for you. Only the chunks connected to it cook: anything not upstream of the Output doesn't run until you wire it back in. Like a View, it has no output port, so nothing can be wired past it. A file saved before Outputs existed keeps its Views and gets no Output added.

  • A View wins while it's active. Looking at a chunk mid-chain cooks only what that View needs. With no active View, the graph cooks to its Output.
  • Picking the Output works like picking a View. Press 1, or double-click the Output's header, to cook to it. Right-click a chunk and choose Set Output to move the Output's wire to that chunk; the graph then cooks to it. The Output is labelled Output [1]: blue while the graph cooks to it, dimmed while a View is active.
  • usdchunks run always cooks to the Output, whichever View the file was saved with. A file with no Output falls back to its active View.
  • A ChunkGroup delivers its Output to the outer graph. Its inner Views are for looking while you're inside it.

The same split exists elsewhere: Nuke's Viewer and Write, Katana's view flag and Render node, Houdini's display flag and Output LOP.

docs.title: Where results land: C-LIVRPS
docs.text:
What a chunk cooks goes under the session layer, the strongest layer of the stage. So a cooked result beats every value authored by hand, in any layer: think of it as a C in front of USD's LIVRPS strength order.

C   chunk results   a later layer's turn beats an earlier one; nearer the Output beats further
L   local layers    shot.usda > lighting.usda > layout.usda ...
I V R R P S         as USD

To change a result, change what the chunk cooks from: its params, which you can override from any layer, or a chunk after it. When several layers bring chunks (a shot sublayering its departments), each layer's chunks cook in turn, weakest layer first, ending at that layer's Output. An Edit Target chunk opts its branch out of C and puts the results into the layer it names, at that layer's place in L.

docs.title: View
docs.text:
In the UI, only chunks connected to the active View cook. From the command line, usdchunks run cooks to the Output instead. A file with neither an Output nor a view cooks everything, and --all cooks everything regardless.

Adding a view: right-click the chunk whose output you want to see and choose Set View 2 or Set View 3. If that view already exists it's reconnected to this chunk; otherwise it's created and connected. Either way it becomes active. The slot already looking at the chunk is shown ticked.

For example: build Mesh → Transform, right-click Transform and choose Set View 2. Move the Transform's sliders and the viewport updates. Only Mesh and Transform cook, because nothing else is connected to the view.

Switching between views: a graph can have up to two views, numbered 2 and 3, since 1 is the Output. Press 2 or 3 to switch to a view, and 1 to go back to the Output. Pressing a number with nothing behind it does nothing, so you can't blank the graph by accident.

The active view has an orange header, and the others are dimmed. Each graph level (the top level, or the inside of a ChunkGroup) has its own two views. When you open a saved file, the view that was active when you saved is active again.

docs.title: ChunkGroup
docs.text:
A ChunkGroup is an empty box you build inside. Add one, double-click to go inside, and work the same way as at the top level. Its only param is doc, a text field for describing what's inside, so someone opening the file (a teammate, or an AI) doesn't have to open the group to find out.

Good to know before you build one:

  • It's real USD nesting. The chunks inside are stored directly under the group's prim, at /chunks/<Group>/<Child>, so the outer graph stays clean.
  • The group's output comes from its Output. A group with no Output (an older file) falls back to the active View inside it, then to the end of its chain.
  • To show an inner param on the outside, loft it. Lofting adds the inner param as a real param on the group node. The connection goes up, from the inner param to the group node. It's not the same as a normal @Node.param@ link between two chunks, so treat lofts separately. A vector (Focus Point, Clipping Range) lofts as one, with all its fields: right-click its header and choose Loft up.
  • To show a whole chunk on the outside, loft the chunk. Right-click it and choose Loft up chunk. Its full panel then shows on the group's Params page, and in the group's section on the page above. Unlike lofting a param, it adds no params or ports to the group: it's one chunk:lofted flag on the chunk's prim. Unloft chunk takes it back off.
  • Groups can be saved as files and loaded back as a sublayer, reference or payload, using plain USD composition. A chunk loaded this way is locked: it has an amber header and can't be moved (auto-layout works around it). You can still change its params. Your changes are written as an over in your own edit target, and the shared file isn't touched.

A chunk with GroupFlags.CONTEXT is shown as a workspace that holds other chunks, not as a node. The top-level tab and ChunkGroup both have it. Output and View don't: they're normal chunks at the end of a chain, not containers. In the Qt frontend, a CONTEXT chunk is shown as a tab. See Writing a graph frontend if you're building this for another host.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This example shows most common operations of working with chunks. In the main() function, we build the parameters and the chunk itself, adding our callbacks.

from usd_chunks import chunk, chunk_core, chunk_notice, chunk_registry
from functools import wraps


def nice_print(func):
    @wraps(func)
    def _wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        begin = f"{'-' * 10}* {func.__qualname__} *{'-' * 10}"
        end = "-" * len(begin)
        print(begin)
        res = func(*args, **kwargs)
        print(end, "\n")
        return res
    return _wrapper


@nice_print
def chunkChanged(owner, notice, sender):
    # Just print some info
    def get_chunk_str(s):
        if isinstance(s, chunk.Chunk):
            return "Chunk"

        if isinstance(s, chunk.Group):
            return "Group"

        if isinstance(s, chunk.Vector):
            return "Vector"

        if isinstance(s, chunk_core.ChunkParamBase):
            return s.evaluate_type().name

        if isinstance(s, chunk_core.AttributeSender):
            return "Attribute"

    msg = f"Chunk Changed: {sender.name} -> {notice.__class__.__name__}"

    step = 4
    indent = step

    for n, s in sender.iter_changes():
        msg += "\n" + " " * indent + f"{get_chunk_str(s)}: {s.name} -> {n.__class__.__name__}"

        if isinstance(s, chunk_core.AttributeSender):
            msg += f": [New Value] = {s.value}"
        indent += step
    print(msg)


@nice_print
def paramChanged(owner, notice, sender):
    print(sender.name, sender.value)


@nice_print
def paramValueChanged(owner, notice, sender: chunk_notice.ChunkNoticePropagator):
    print(notice, sender)


@nice_print
def clickedButton(owner, notice, sender):
    print("Button clicked: ", owner.name)


@nice_print
def primSelectionChanged(owner, notice: chunk_notice.PrimSelectionChangedNotice, sender: chunk_notice.SceneSender):
    print("Prim selection changed: ", notice.data.value)


@nice_print
def propSelectionChanged(owner, notice: chunk_notice.PropSelectionChangedNotice, sender: chunk_notice.SceneSender):
    print("Prop selection changed: ", notice.data.value)


def updateLabel(owner : chunk.Label, notice: chunk_notice.PrimSelectionChangedNotice, sender: chunk_notice.SceneSender):
    """An example callback function that updates the value of the chunkItem to the selected prim path when a new selection occurs

    Args:
        chunkItem (chunk.ChunkParam): The ChunkParamaBase object that was used to to add this callback
        notice (chunk_notice.PropSelectionChangedNotice): The notice object. This is just an identifier for the type of notice sent
        sender (chunk_notice.UsdviewSelectionNotice): The actual sender
    """

    if not notice.data:
        return
    path = notice.data[0].GetPath()
    if path.isEmpty:
        return

    owner.value = str(path)


def main():
    # A simple checkbox
    checkbox = chunk.Checkbox("enable")

    # A simple callback. This is called whenever anything on the checkbox is changed
    #     checkbox.add_callback(paramChanged)

    # A more explicit callback. Only triggers paramChanged when checkbox.value changes
    #     checkbox.add_callback(paramValueChanged, sender=checkbox.get_attribute_sender("value"))

    # A slider with horizontal layout
    slider = chunk.Slider("slider")

    # Change the layout flag to modify the layout
    #   slider = chunk.Slider("slider", layout=chunk.ChunkFlags.LayoutFlags.VERTICAL)

    # A ChunkParamGroup is a container of ChunkParams or other ChunkParamGroups
    sliderGroup = chunk.Group("SliderGroup")

    # Adding a callback on a group will by default call method when anything on the group changes, i.e any child params updated
    #   sliderGroup.add_callback(groupChanged)

    # One can also be more explicit when adding callbacks, for example only listening to attribute changed notices.
    # Any child of this group will send this notice, and iteratively send it again with every owner as a sender.
    # Sending the notice through the hierarchy allows doing this:
    #   sliderGroup.add_callback(paramValueChanged, notice_alias=chunk_notice.ChunkNoticeAlias.ATTRIBUTE_CHANGED)
    # instead of this:
    #   sliderGroup.add_callback(paramValueChanged, sender=sliderGroup.get_param("slider").get_attribute_sender("value"))
    # The difference being we can subscribe to all ATTRIBUTE_CHANGED notices instead of only the ones sent from the specified sender.

    # Make the group collapsable and labeled. Flags and states can be combined with bitwise operator:
    #   & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ~ (NOT)
    sliderGroup.set_flag(chunk.ChunkFlags.GroupFlags.COLLAPSABLE | chunk.ChunkFlags.GroupFlags.FRAMED)

    # Similarly, flags and states can be unset
    #   sliderGroup.unset_flag(chunk.ChunkFlags.GroupFlags.COLLAPSABLE)

    # Sets the sliderGroup to collapsed by default.
    sliderGroup.set_state(chunk.ChunkFlags.State.COLLAPSED)

    # Groups default layout flags are LABELED | FRAMED
    # Chunks default layout flags are LABELED | FRAMED | COLLAPSABLE

    # In order to add the same param multiple times to a chunk, use clone(). This will copy the param and its
    # attributes. Connections / callbacks will not be copied.
    # In order to retrieve the new instances of the slider, you'll need to retrieve it from the group as such:
    #    slider = sliderGroup.getParam("slider1")
    # Duplicate param names will be suffixed with an index. First instance of a param will not be suffixed.
    # This results in these params on the group:
    #   ('slider', 'slider1', 'slider2')
    sliderGroup.add_params([slider, slider.clone(), slider.clone()])

    # A vector is an extension of the group, with a single param repeated length times. The suffix replace the default
    # numbered suffix for duplicated params. Accessing params on a vector can be done with __setitem__ (vec["sliderX"] or vec[0])
    # as well as get_param() and similar group functions
    sliderVec = chunk.Vector("SliderVec", param=chunk.Slider(), length=3, suffixes="XYZ")
    sliderVec[0] = 10

    # A button will call the callback just like any other param, but does not care about its value
    button = chunk.Button("button")
    button.add_callback(clickedButton)

    # Get access to the ChunkRegistry singleton. This is responsible for loading/unloading the chunks, and will send ChunkNoticeAlias.CHUNK_LOADED when a
    # chunk was loaded. It also stores the SceneSender, which sends UI related notices such as PRIM_SELECTION_CHANGED and PROP_SELECTION_CHANGED
    #   reg = chunk_registry.ChunkRegistry()
    # Accessing the scene in this function may result in some errors as the stage is not properly loaded at the time this function
    # runs. So access in to the reg.scene should be reserved to callbacks 

    # A label - Not directly modifiable in the UI
    label = chunk.Label("label")

    # Add the updateLabel as a callback - this will be called whenever the prim selection changes in UsdView. Any UsdView notices will be sent from
    # the chunk_notice.SceneSender. As the label does not emit send the PRIM_SELECTION_CHANGED itself, we need to either specify a sender (the SceneSender in this cas),
    # or listen globally for the notice.
    label.add_callback(
        updateLabel, listen_globally=True, notice_alias=chunk_notice.ChunkNoticeAlias.PRIM_SELECTION_CHANGED
    )

    # A text edit is a parameter for editing strings
    textEdit = chunk.LineEdit("line_edit")

    # A FileBrowser is a LineEdit with a button for launching a File Browser dialog. The filtering of file names
    # is done by appending all extensions to the pattern, so this would result in a filter:
    #   '*.jpg *.png *.tif'
    # If pattern is not set, an asterix '*' will be used. If no extensions are set, the filter will use only the pattern
    fileBrowse = chunk.FileBrowser(
        "line_edit", pattern="*", extensions=[".jpg", ".png", ".tif"], flags=chunk.ChunkFlags.ParamFlags.FILE_EXISTING
    )

    # A simple menu
    menu = chunk.Menu("menu", menu_items=["hello0", "hello1"])
    # By default, the menu enforces its value to exist in the menu_items list, so menu.value = "hello3" would fail
    # validation and revert to default value of menu_items[0]

    # A menu with pictures: Qt shows a searchable grid of tiles, Blender its thumbnail picker,
    # other frontends a plain dropdown. The value is still the item's name. Pictures are paths
    # to local image files; assign a new dict to item_images as they arrive (downloads, say).
    looks = chunk.ImageMenu("look", "Look", menu_items=["Gold", "Oak"],
                            item_images={"Gold": "/path/to/gold.jpg"})

    # A separator holds no value, is just there for the UI.
    sep = chunk.Separator(layout=chunk.ChunkFlags.LayoutFlags.HORIZONTAL)

    # Create the actual chunk - this is in practice just a chunk.Group with some additional behaviour
    myChunk = chunk.Chunk("Hello World", category="Examples")
    myChunk.add_params([label, checkbox, button, sep, textEdit, menu, fileBrowse, sliderGroup, sliderVec])

    # Add a callback. With no arguments, the callback will be called whenever any of the children on the chunk is changed
    myChunk.add_callback(chunkChanged)

    # Prints the hierarchy of the chunk. Useful for debugging chunks
    myChunk.print_hierarchy()

    return myChunk

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
An expression makes one param read its value from another param. It's written in the param's value, like @Box.size@ * 2.

usd_chunks also works with USD's own ${NAME} variables. Those are a different thing and are covered at the end of this page.

docs.title: 🔗 Writing an expression
docs.text:
A reference is @ + chunk name + . + param name + @:

@Box.size@
  • Chunk name is the node's name in the graph, like Box or Transform1.
  • Param name is the param's name, not its label. A param called size with the label "Box Size" is @Box.size@.
  • The param can be inside a group. @Box.size@ still finds it.
  • A Vector can be read as one value: @Box.translate@.
  • A row of a list is read by its index, from 0: @Fence.post[2]@ is the third row's post. It works inside text too: @Fence.post[2]@/geo. Delete a row and refs to the rows after it are renumbered to follow them. A ref to the deleted row is removed, and that param goes back to its default.

docs.title: ✏️ Setting one
docs.text:
Wire it in the graph. Connecting a value port writes @Node.param@ for you.

Number and checkbox params: right-click the param and choose Set Expression.... Type the expression and press OK. To remove it, right-click and choose Clear Expression. That puts the param back to its default.

Text params (like a prim path): type the expression straight into the field.

A param with an expression has a blue, italic label. Hover the label to see the expression. A number or checkbox field shows the result. A text field shows the expression.

From Python: set .value to the text. .value gives the result, .raw_value gives the text.

node.get_param("height").value = "@Box.size@ * 2"
node.get_param("height").value      # 20.0
node.get_param("height").raw_value  # "@Box.size@ * 2"

docs.title: ➗ Maths
docs.text:
On a number param the expression is worked out as a sum. You can use +, -, *, /, //, %, ** and brackets, with plain numbers and @refs@:

@Box.size@ * 2
(@Box.size@ + @Lid.height@) / 2
-@Box.size@
  • An int param gives a whole number. The decimal part is cut off, so 10.4 becomes 10.
  • Only the operators above work. Functions like sin() and comparisons like > don't. If it can't be worked out (this includes dividing by zero), the param gets the text instead of a number.

docs.title: 🔤 Building text
docs.text:
On a text param each @ref@ is swapped for its value. Use it to build a path or a name:

@Box.primpath_location@/lid

If Box's prim path is /World/box, this gives /World/box/lid.

A number is written the way Python prints it. A float 3.0 becomes 3.0, not 3.

docs.title: 📌 Good to know
docs.text:
• It updates live. Change Box.size and every param that reads it updates.
  • Same graph only. An expression can only reach chunks in the same graph. A chunk inside a ChunkGroup can't read a chunk outside it, or the other way round. To pass a value in or out, right-click the param's label and choose Loft up (see ChunkGroup).
  • Renames are followed. Renaming a chunk or a param updates every expression that points at it, right away and in the USD.
  • Wrong names are ignored. If @Box.size@ can't be found, the log says Expression ref @Box.size@ not found. A lone @Box.size@ then gives the param's default.
  • Loops are stopped. If A reads B and B reads A, the log says Expression cycle and the params keep their old values.
  • It's saved in the USD. Each @ref@ is a USD connection on the chunk prim. A text param stores the expression as its value. Any other param stores the result as its value and the expression text in customData under chunk:expression.

docs.title: 🌐 Stage variables (${NAME})
docs.text:
These are USD's expression variables, not a usd_chunks feature. They live on the stage, not on a chunk. You set them with the Stage Expression chunk (stage_expression): add a row with a name, a type and a value. It writes them to the session layer, so the file you opened isn't changed.

USD only reads ${NAME} in asset paths and variant selections. The asset path must be a whole USD expression: in backticks, with the path in double quotes. For example, in an Inline USD chunk (inline_usd):

#usda 1.0

def Xform "Set" (
    references = @`"/assets/set_${SHOT}.usda"`@
)
{
}

Change SHOT on the Stage Expression chunk and the reference switches to the other file. Without the backticks, USD looks for a file literally called set_${SHOT}.usda.

The file fields on Reference, Payload and Sublayer don't take a ${NAME} path yet. They check that the file exists, and a path with ${SHOT} in it doesn't.

  • ${NAME} in a param that isn't a file path stays as plain text, and the log warns you. Inline USD also logs this warning, but its text goes to USD as it is, so the reference still works.
  • To run a different part of the graph based on a variable, use the Stage Expression Switch chunk (stage_expression_switch). Pick the variable and type a pattern like sh01* sh02*. If it matches, the lower input runs. If not, the upper input runs.
  • A variable can be a string, int, bool or list of strings. There is no float.
  • If you add a variable that didn't exist when the stage was opened, a reference that already failed to load won't pick it up. Reopen the stage. Changing an existing variable works live.

docs.title: Making a chunk fast
docs.text:
In short: a slow cook is almost always one of two things. Either it authors through the Usd API one call at a time, or it loops over data in Python. Write specs with sdf_authoring inside one Sdf.ChangeBlock, and do the maths with numpy. Threads don't help; see What doesn't help.

This page is for writing or speeding up a chunk's execute(). The numbers come from benchmarks on the usdbundle build (USD 26.05, Python 3.11) in October 2026.

docs.title: Find where the time goes
docs.text:
Measure before you change anything. Wrap the cook in cProfile or time its parts with time.perf_counter(). Cooks usually spend their time in one of these:

Symptom Cause Fix Time scales with prims or attributes written; profile full of DefinePrim, CreateAttribute, Set One change notice per authoring call Write specs Many attr.Set(value, time) calls, one per frame One notice per sample sim_bake.write_samples Time scales with points or faces; profile full of Gf.Vec3f, Matrix4d.Transform, list comprehensions Python loops over data numpy Nested loops comparing every element with every other O(n²) search A k-d tree

docs.title: Write specs, not Usd API calls
docs.text:
Every Usd API call that authors something sends a change notice: stage.DefinePrim, prim.CreateAttribute, attr.Set, UsdGeom.Mesh.Define, AddTransformOp. For each notice the stage recomposes, and everything listening runs: the framework, usdview's prim tree and the viewport. A handful of calls is fine. Thousands are the whole cook.

On 8,000 prims with three attributes each, cooked through the framework:

Usd API Sdf, one ChangeBlock Cook 3.9 s 0.2 s Next frame, Storm 0.22 s 0.05 s Next frame, V-Ray 1.6 s 0.07 s

Converting CAD Import made it 9.6× faster on 3,000 placements.

usd_chunks.sdf_authoring writes specs directly into the layer the stage's edit target points at, at the path the edit target maps to. They land where the Usd API would have put them, including inside a variant:

from pxr import Gf, Sdf, UsdGeom
from usd_chunks import sdf_authoring


def execute(node):
    stage = node.get_stage()
    writer = sdf_authoring.Writer(stage)
    with Sdf.ChangeBlock():
        for i, (x, y, z) in enumerate(positions):
            spec = writer.define(f"/World/Rocks/R{i}", "Cube")
            sdf_authoring.attribute(spec, "size", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Double, 0.5)
            sdf_authoring.transform(spec, Gf.Matrix4d().SetTranslate(Gf.Vec3d(x, y, z)))
            sdf_authoring.primvar(spec, "displayColor", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Color3fArray,
                                  [Gf.Vec3f(1, 0, 0)], UsdGeom.Tokens.constant)
Usd API sdf_authoring stage.DefinePrim(path, type), UsdGeom.X.Define writer.define(path, type) A property on a prim this layer doesn't define yet writer.over(path) prim.GetReferences().AddInternalReference(path) writer.reference(spec, path) CreateXAttr(value) on a schema attribute(spec, name, type, value) prim.CreateAttribute(name, type) attribute(spec, name, type, custom=True) PrimvarsAPI.CreatePrimvar(name, type, interp).Set(v) primvar(spec, name, type, v, interp) AddTransformOp().Set(m) on a fresh prim transform(spec, m) prim.SetInstanceable(True) spec.instanceable = True

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Don't read back what you wrote inside the block. Composition catches up when the block closes. Inside it, a prim you defined isn't on the stage yet. Reading anything else is fine, including upstream prims and the source of a copy. If the loop needs composed state (a world transform, the prim it just made), gather it in a pass before the block.
  • Make the Writer inside the author_in_variant_contexts loop. It reads the edit target once, when it's created.
  • Get variability right. Attributes a schema declares uniform need uniform=True: subdivisionScheme, xformOpOrder, orientation, and a GeomSubset's elementType and familyName. The Usd API gets this from the schema. Specs don't.
  • Match custom. Schema attributes and primvars aren't custom (the default). Prim.CreateAttribute makes custom ones, so pass custom=True when replacing it.
  • Compare outputs when you convert. Run the old and new code on the same input and compare layer.ExportToString(). CAD Import, Duplicate Prim and Semantic Labels were converted this way with byte-identical results. tests/test_sdf_authoring.py shows the pattern.

Leave the Usd API alone where it's a fixed handful of calls per cook (a root prim, a scope, one material). It's clearer, and there's nothing to gain.

docs.title: Time samples
docs.text: To write many frames, use sim_bake.write_samples(attr, ((time, value), ...), default=...). It writes every sample into the edit target's layer in one change block. One attr.Set(v, t) per frame cost a breakage preview 3 s for 7,000 notices.

docs.title: Do the maths in numpy
docs.text:
numpy runs a whole array in C, while a Python loop pays interpreter overhead per element. On point and face data the difference is usually 10–100×.

Move data between USD and numpy with FromNumpy, not lists:

points = np.asarray(mesh.GetPointsAttr().Get())              # Vt -> (N, 3) array
attr.Set(Vt.Vec3fArray.FromNumpy(points.astype(np.float32)))  # array -> Vt, no Python loop

Vt.Vec3fArray([Gf.Vec3f(*p) for p in points]) builds one Python object per point. Avoid it.

Transform points with one matrix product. Gf.Matrix4d uses row vectors: p' = p · M, with the translation in the last row. So:

m = np.asarray(xform_cache.GetLocalToWorldTransform(prim))
world = points @ m[:3, :3] + m[3, :3]   # same as m.Transform(p) for every point

usd_chunks.mesh_math.world_points(prim, points) does exactly this. Its sibling fan_triangulate(counts, indices) returns (triangles, corners, face_of_triangle) for any polygon mesh. Use both instead of writing the loop again.

Watch these details:

  • dtypes. USD point arrays are float32. Do the maths in float64 if precision matters, and convert once when writing (astype(np.float32)), not per element.
  • Quaternions. Vt.QuathArray.FromNumpy / QuatfArray.FromNumpy take [x, y, z, w], imaginary first. MuJoCo and most maths code use [w, x, y, z]. Roll the last axis (np.roll(q, -1, axis=-1)) before writing.
  • Contiguous arrays. FromNumpy needs a C-contiguous array, so call np.ascontiguousarray after slicing or transposing.

docs.title: Seeded randomness
docs.text:
Users rely on a seed giving the same result every time, so a speed-up must never change what a seed produces.

  • Don't batch or reorder random draws in existing code. If a loop calls rng.random() per attempt, vectorizing the maths around it is fine. Pre-drawing the numbers into an array changes the result unless the draws stay in exactly the same order, including draws that only happen on some attempts.
  • New code: use np.random.default_rng(seed) and draw whole arrays (rng.random((n, 3))). It's fast and reproducible from the start. Never use the global np.random or random module: anything else drawing from it changes your result.

docs.title: Nearest neighbours
docs.text:
Checking every point against every other is O(n²), which takes seconds at a few thousand points. Use scipy.spatial.cKDTree, and keep scipy optional the way Scatter Points does:

try:
    from scipy.spatial import cKDTree
except ImportError:
    cKDTree = None  # fall back to the slower path

For a few hundred points, numpy broadcasting is enough: d2 = ((a[:, None] - b[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).

Some loops are sequential by nature, like dart throwing where each sample depends on the last or a simulation step. Vectorize across the independent elements inside each step instead, for example every particle in one step.

docs.title: What doesn't help
docs.text:
These were measured and rejected, so you don't have to try them again:

  • Threads. Two independent cooks in two threads ran at 0.83× (Usd API) and 0.96× (Sdf), slower than one after the other. USD's Python bindings hold the GIL. numpy is already multithreaded inside, so two numpy threads ran at 0.33×. Only waiting (subprocesses, I/O, renders) overlaps in threads. For wide independent work like wedges and sweeps, use processes.
  • Authoring into a detached layer and swapping it in. 1.1–1.2×. The cost is the per-call notice, not which stage hears it.
  • Usd API calls inside a Sdf.ChangeBlock. Not safe: a prim defined inside the block isn't composed yet, so the next Usd call on it fails or misbehaves. Use specs.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
1. Profile first: authoring or maths?
  2. Authoring that grows with the data → sdf_authoring in one ChangeBlock, time samples through write_samples.
  3. Python loops over points, faces or instances → numpy, plus FromNumpy, plus mesh_math.
  4. Pairwise searches → cKDTree (optional import) or broadcasting.
  5. Seeded output unchanged? Compare before and after with the same seed.
  6. Output unchanged? Compare layer.ExportToString() before and after.

docs.title: Chunk gizmos: the host contract
docs.text:
How a DCC displays chunk-driven viewport handles.

usd_chunks records. The DCC interprets. This repo authors a schema onto chunk prims and owns the write-back. It does not draw, pick, or drag. If you are building a viewport layer — usd-guides for usdview and Kraken, or a native integration for Houdini, Blender or Maya — this page is the whole surface you need.

The governing rule everything here is designed around:

A host must be able to build a native handle from ui:gizmo:* alone, with no geometry library from us.

Three of the five target hosts have manipulators better than anything we would ship, so our geometry would be a downgrade there. Nothing below asks you to draw our shapes.

docs.title: The four calls
docs.text:
chunk_gizmo.resolve_gizmos(prim) -> list[GizmoDesc]   # what handles exist
chunk_gizmo.apply_bindings(chunk_prim, name, value)   # write-back
chunk.start_gizmo() / chunk.stop_gizmo()              # drag bracket

Plus two optional helpers:

chunk_gizmo.decompose(matrix) -> {"translate": Vec3d, "rotate": Vec3d, "scale": Vec3d}
chunk_gizmo.ensure_transform_chunk(prim) -> GizmoDesc | None   # see §8

That is all of it. There is no callback to register, no base class to subclass, and nothing we call on you.

docs.title: 1. Discovery: from a selected prim to its handles
docs.text:
The user selects /World/Cube. The handles are declared on a chunk prim under /chunks, which is not in the viewport and is not what anyone clicks. Two routes:

Route A — ask us.

for desc in chunk_gizmo.resolve_gizmos(selected_prim):
    ...

Walks the prim's layer stack. Every chunk owns its own Sdf.Layer, so a prim's spec stack already records which chunks authored it. Cheap, and a disabled or muted chunk drops out for free because its specs are not in the stack.

Also accepts a chunk prim directly, for a node-graph-driven UI.

Route B — pure USD, no dependency on this repo.

Index every prim carrying a ui:gizmo:*:anchor relationship, and find the ones whose targets include your selection. Slower — O(chunks) per selection change, which is nothing at realistic graph sizes — but it means a third-party host is never forced to import usd_chunks just to find handles.

Write-back still needs us. See §5.

A handle only appears after the chunk has cooked at least once. Route A traces through the layer that a cook writes; before that the layer is empty and there is nothing to trace. Chunks cook on creation, so this is rarely visible — but if handles are missing on a freshly loaded scene, this is why.

Order is meaningful: nearest the view first. resolve_gizmos returns handles sorted by exec depth, so descs[0] is the chunk with the final say over that prim. A host with no chunk selected can drive descs[0] and be editing the one the user can actually see.

Sorted by the graph rather than by layer strength, because the two disagree in one case that matters: a chunk which has not authored anything yet is not in the prim's layer stack at all. An Offset Transform sitting at zero authors nothing by design, so it would sort last however far downstream it sat -- and ownership would flip the moment someone typed a number into it.

Which handle belongs to whom. resolve_gizmos returns handles from every chunk in the prim's layer stack, upstream ones included. You filter to the chunk the user has selected, if your UI has a notion of one. A prim touched by two transform chunks in one chain would otherwise show two identical handles in the same place. Stated the other way round: a handle only ever edits the chunk you are looking at.

docs.title: 2. The record
docs.text:
GizmoDesc is a plain data record. No Qt types, no callbacks, nothing beyond pxr.

field type meaning name str Identity within the chunk. The namespace segment, never the type — two cubes on one chunk is ordinary. type str What kind of handle, and what it sends back. See §3. label str Display name. Falls back to the chunk's name. chunk_prim Sdf.Path Which chunk declared this handle. Pass it straight back to apply_bindings, and use it to filter to the chunk the user selected. name is not unique across chunks — more than one calls its handle transform. anchor tuple[Sdf.Path] The scene prims the handle hangs off. Already resolved — never a param to evaluate. anchor_source str The param that produced them. For our write-back; you do not need it. driver tuple[Sdf.Path] The properties this handle writes, in order. Informational — write through apply_bindings, not directly. axis str \| None Signed direction token, in the anchor's local space. None means free drag. space str "local" or "world". Defaults to "local" and is only authored when non-default. editmode tuple[str] When to show it. See §4. offset tuple[float,float,float] \| None Where the handle sits, as a point in the anchor's own space. None means you decide — put it on the geometry. Not static: a chunk can move it between resolves. size float \| None Relative size hint. None means you decide — usually the right answer, since a viewport wants a screen-constant handle and only you know the camera distance.

A chunk can suppress one of its own handles while a mode of its own would fight it — camera.py hides its transform handle while lock_to_freecam is on, because the freecam re-authors the transform every frame and a drag would silently snap back. resolve_gizmos simply does not return a suppressed handle, so route A needs no check. Route B must honour ui:gizmo:<name>:hidden = true, which is authored for exactly this purpose.

Several anchor targets means one handle at their averaged pivot, not one handle per target. A transform chunk pointed at three prims is ordinary use.

docs.title: Where to draw it
docs.text:
The anchor says what the handle is attached to. It is not always where the handle sits.

Read the driven value and offset by it. Follow the driver connections, read the current values, and place the handle accordingly:

  • A translate handle driving an offset — "shift this body 3 units from its start" — belongs at anchor + (3, 0, 0). Drawn on the anchor it would sit at zero and never move.
  • A cube on focus distance with axis = "-Z" belongs at the focus point, distance along the camera's -Z. That is where the existing focus reticle already draws.

The rule is the same in both cases: the handle shows the value, and the anchor is the frame that value is measured in. offset is a point on top of that — not a substitute for reading the value.

offset is a pivot, and it is not static. A Transform chunk with a pivot set reports it here, so:

  • offset is None — no chunk has an opinion. Place the handle yourself, and put it on the geometry rather than on the transform origin: those differ more often than they look like they should. A Kitchen_set cup carries a transform on its group and very nearly the inverse on the mesh, so its world transform composes to the identity and its origin is out at the world origin. The bbox centroid is the answer that stays useful.
  • offset set — draw there, and make your rotation turn about it. It is a point in the anchor's own object space, so map it through the anchor's local-to-world: primWorld.Transform(offset). The chunk's op is the innermost one, so everything upstream of it still applies to the pivot.

The value moves while the user drags a pivot slider, so re-read it on stage change rather than caching it at selection time. Nothing else about the drag changes: you still report the absolute matrix the user dragged to, and the chunk solves its own params about its own pivot.

docs.title: Letting the user drag the pivot
docs.text:
Optional, and the reason offset has a write counterpart. Hold a modifier (usdview's gizmo uses D, matching its Maya-ish W/E/R/M) and a drag moves the pivot rather than the object:

chunk_gizmo.apply_offset(desc.chunk_prim, desc.name, world_point)   # -> bool

You send a world point. You have a position under the mouse and nothing else; you do not know that a Transform chunk keeps its pivot in the anchor's object space, and you should not have to. The conversion happens on our side, exactly as apply_bindings takes an absolute matrix and lets the chunk work out its own share.

Three rules:

  • False means do nothing. Unlike commit_transform, do not fall back to writing the prim — there is nowhere on a prim to put a pivot, and moving the prim instead is the opposite of what was asked. False just means no chunk here owns a pivot.
  • Write every tick, never batch to mouse-release. The chunk cooks per write, and that is what keeps the object still while the pivot moves under it. Same rule as every other drag.
  • Reset your handle when the gesture ends. A pivot drag leaves your manipulator holding the whole drag in its local translation; carry that into the next ordinary drag and the object jumps by however far the pivot moved.

A chunk that does not implement the write hook returns False, so this degrades to "no pivot dragging" rather than to anything surprising.

docs.title: 3. Types, and what each one sends back
docs.text:
A gizmo drives exactly one thing, and its type says what. There is no slot, no key, no payload map — reading the type answers the whole question.

type you send back drives transform Gf.Matrix4d Nine params: translate xyz, rotate xyz, scale xyz translate Gf.Vec3d Three params, or one vector-typed param rotate Gf.Vec3d, Euler XYZ, degrees as above scale Gf.Vec3d as above cube, sphere a single number One param box six numbers Six params: the +X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z faces, in that order

transform is the whole-chunk handle — in effect "run your native transform manipulator and give me the result". Build your own TRS handle, let the user drag it, and hand back the matrix it produced. You never need to decompose it; we do that, so the Euler convention lives in exactly one place instead of being re-derived slightly differently in every host.

Shape types are one-dimensional handles. A shape plus an axis is a linear handle: map it onto your native linear-handle primitive and ignore the shape name entirely. usd-guides draws the shape literally; Houdini and Blender should not.

box is a box whose faces are the handles. Draw no handle of your own. Each driven param is the distance from the anchor's origin to one face, in the anchor's local space, so the six values are the box. The user hovers a face, it highlights, they grab it and pull it along its normal; only that face moves. Two pure helpers do the maths, in the anchor's space (apply the inverse of its world transform to the mouse ray first):

hit = chunk_gizmo.pick_box_face(values, origin, direction)  # on hover and press
if hit:
    face, t = hit
    start, grab = values, origin + direction * t            # keep both for the drag
...
new = chunk_gizmo.drag_box_face(start, face, grab, origin, direction)  # every tick
chunk_gizmo.apply_bindings(desc.chunk_prim, desc.name, new)

Pick against the box, never the scene. pick_box_face tests the box the six values describe, so a mesh inside the volume can never be what is grabbed. Test it before your own pick and let a hit win. drag_box_face always starts from the press's values and grab point, not the last tick's, so a long drag does not drift. Snapping is the chunk's (gizmo_changed), not yours.

Unknown types. The set will grow. Skip a type you do not recognise rather than guessing — a custom type is one only the usd-guides render path understands, and silently mis-drawing it is worse than not drawing it.

docs.title: axis
docs.text:
X, -X, Y, -Y, Z, -Z, screen — in the anchor's local space.

The sign is load-bearing. Camera focus distance is -Z, because a camera looks down -Z. An unsigned token would put that handle out the back of the camera.

None (attribute absent) means free drag: any mouse direction moves the driven value, and you choose the mapping. Sensitivity needs no schema — numeric params carry min_value / max_value, so scale screen delta against the declared range.

Resolve the token to a world direction from the anchor's matrix, which you already hold in order to draw. Deliberately not a vector: one authored in world space would be wrong the moment the anchor rotates.

docs.title: 4. When to show a handle: editmode
docs.text:
A token[], because a handle wanting more than one is normal.

value show it when onPrimSelection your viewport selection includes the anchor prim onChunkSelection the chunk itself is selected — node graph, or a LOP node always the chunk is live

Defaults to ["onPrimSelection"].

You apply this against a selection you already own. Nothing pushes at you and there is no activation call to implement. onChunkSelection is defined but not yet wired on our side — treat it as reserved.

docs.title: 5. Write-back
docs.text:
chunk.start_gizmo()
while dragging:
    chunk_gizmo.apply_bindings(desc.chunk_prim, desc.name, value)   # every tick
chunk.stop_gizmo()

apply_bindings takes either the chunk prim path off the record or a live chunk object, so a host that only ever holds GizmoDesc needs no lookup of its own.

docs.title: Do not write the prim directly
docs.text:
It will be erased. A chunk like transform.py rewrites its whole layer, its xformOp:transform included, on every cook, so a direct write survives until the next execute and then vanishes. Nor should you write the inputs: attributes in driver yourself — those are param storage, and going around the param system skips the propagation that makes downstream chunks update.

apply_bindings writes the params, which dirties the chunk, which recooks, which moves the prim. That is the whole reason this boundary exists.

docs.title: Write on every tick
docs.text:
Never batch writes to stop_gizmo() yourself. Call apply_bindings every tick; usd_chunks decides when to cook.

Batching in the host is the tempting optimisation the first time a heavy chunk cooks slowly, and for a chunk that cooks fast it is exactly what makes a handle feel dead: the object stops following the cursor and jumps at the end. Writing per tick is already how sliders behave.

Inside the start_gizmo()/stop_gizmo() bracket, usd_chunks paces the cooks:

  • At most every chunk_gizmo.DRAG_INTERVAL (1/30 s), the newest value only. A write that comes sooner waits on a scene.call_later timer and is replaced by any later one, so mouse moves that arrive during a cook collapse into one cook instead of queueing behind it. A tick that arrives once the interval is up cooks then and there, so the drag keeps cooking even where a host's timers starve while input keeps coming (Qt's on Windows do); the timer only cooks the value left when the mouse stops.
  • Once a cook takes longer than chunk_gizmo.SLOW_COOK (50 ms), not until release. A cook that long blocks the viewport, so the handle would freeze on every one. While the handle moves the rest of the drag cooks nothing; it cooks where the handle rests (held still for chunk_gizmo.DRAG_REST, 0.1 s; each tick starts the wait again) and where it is let go. That release cook is timed too, and the chunk's next drag starts from it: still slow, it waits from the first tick; fast again, it drags live.

stop_gizmo() cooks the write still waiting before GIZMO_STOP goes out. Outside a bracket, every write cooks at once.

Draw your handle from the mouse every frame, not from the cooked prim: it would trail the cursor by up to one interval plus a cook, and on a slow chunk stand still until release. Your call_later must honour its delay, and your viewport must redraw after a cook that a timer ran, not only on mouse moves.

docs.title: Notices
docs.text:
GIZMO_START → GIZMO_CHANGED (one per cook, after the write) → GIZMO_STOP.

If your host has its own undo stack, open a block on START and close it on STOP. usdview needs none of this: chunk_undo.UndoStack (fed by frontends/qt/undo.py) makes one step of everything from a mouse press to the next input, so a drag is one undo whether its writes came from a handle, a slider or a cook. It undoes chunk prims only (docs/undo.md); with the C++ usd-undo plugin loaded, that one owns Ctrl+Z instead and coalesces at Sdf level, as it does in Kraken.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• An unknown gizmo name raises — you asked for a handle the chunk does not declare.
  • A wrong-arity value raises before writing anything, so a bad drag cannot leave a chunk half-updated.
  • Some chunks solve their own drags (a lookat point has no param to bind to). This is invisible to you: same call, same payload.

docs.title: 6. Conventions not inferable from the USD
docs.text:
Three things you cannot read off the attributes. They are here because a host that guesses gets them silently wrong.

  1. The transform driver is ordered translate, rotate, scale. Nine connections. The arity is discoverable by counting; the order is not. Only matters if you bypass apply_bindings, which you should not.
  2. Absent space means local. Only authored when non-default, to keep the usda quiet.
  3. Absent size means you decide. Not "size 1".

docs.title: 7. Graceful degradation
docs.text: A DCC that has never heard of ui:gizmo: ignores the attributes completely. They are plain uniform token attributes and one relationship on a prim it already ignores. There is no plugin to register and nothing breaks.

docs.title: 8. A prim no chunk drives
docs.text:
resolve_gizmos returns nothing for a prim that no chunk touches — an imported mesh, a cube from a sublayer. The obvious fallback is to write the prim directly, and it is the wrong one: that edit is not in the graph, so it does not survive the driving chunk's next cook and it is not what gets written out when the scene is saved. The user moved something and nothing recorded it.

desc = chunk_gizmo.ensure_transform_chunk(prim)   # creates one if nothing offers a handle
if desc:
    chunk_gizmo.apply_bindings(desc.chunk_prim, desc.name, matrix)

Same idea as Houdini dropping an Edit node in front of geometry you start moving. We decide what to create and where it lands in the graph, so a host never learns the /chunks layout:

  • Only when nothing already places the prim. The test is placement_gizmos(prim) — any handle of type transform, translate, rotate or scale. Not "is there a Transform chunk", and deliberately not "is there a transform handle" either: rbd_solver declares separate translate and rotate offsets and no scale, so it can never form a whole-chunk transform, yet it plainly owns where that body starts. Testing only for transform reported such a prim as unowned and stacked a duplicate chunk on top of it. Declaring any placement handle is how a chunk opts out.
  • A prim can be owned without offering one matrix-taking handle. ensure_transform_chunk then returns None having created nothing — that is "owned by parts", not "unowned". Drive the parts individually: decompose(matrix) keys by gizmo type, so each entry goes to the handle of that type, and a type with no handle is simply not written.
  • At the end of the active context's chain, wired to the tail, with any view moved along to it — the same placement as creating it by hand in the Params tab.
  • Seeded from the prim's current local transform, so the object does not jump when the chunk appears.
  • Idempotent. Safe to call once per mouse-move; the second call resolves the chunk the first one made.
  • Returns None if it could not create one (no transform module, no live scene). Decide for yourself whether that is fatal or a reason to fall back to writing the prim.

Call it at grab time if you have a drag-start hook, so the creation lands inside your undo bracket. Calling it on the first commit works too, one frame later.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
Selecting /World/Cube, which a Transform chunk drives:

uniform token   ui:gizmo:transform:type     = "transform"
uniform token   ui:gizmo:transform:label    = "Transform"
uniform token[] ui:gizmo:transform:editmode = ["onPrimSelection"]
rel             ui:gizmo:transform:anchor   = </World/Cube>
uniform token   ui:gizmo:transform:driver.connect = [ ...nine params... ]

A Houdini integration, with no geometry from us:

  1. Selection changes → resolve_gizmos(selected_prim) (or the anchor-rel index).
  2. Filter to the selected chunk.
  3. editmode contains onPrimSelection and the anchor matches → show it.
  4. type == "transform" → build the native TRS handle; label names it.
  5. Place it at the anchor prim's world transform. Several anchors → their averaged pivot.
  6. Press → chunk.start_gizmo(), open an undo block.
  7. Each drag tick → apply_bindings(chunk, "transform", handle_matrix).
  8. Release → chunk.stop_gizmo(), close the block.

The user sees the cube follow the handle, because step 7 wrote nine float params and the chunk recooked.

docs.title: Writing a graph frontend
docs.text:
The node graph is split in two. The engine (usd_chunks.graph.engine) decides what happens to the graph; a frontend decides what appears on screen and how input arrives. The engine imports no toolkit — a test asserts that in a subprocess — so a frontend can be written for any of them.

There are four today, deliberately different in shape:

frontends.qt.nodegraph frontends.flet.nodegraph frontends.imgui.nodegraph frontends.blender.nodegraph Drawing QGraphicsItems that place themselves canvas primitives recomputed each refresh redrawn every frame none — Blender draws the tree Node bodies real ChunkWidgets via proxy widgets real Flet controls in a Stack drawn inline per frame RNA properties, on their input socket (rest via draw_buttons) Hit-testing the scene does it the view does it (port_at, node_at) imgui_node_editor does it Blender does it Positions on the item, written back to USD on the view, written back to USD owned by the editor once placed on the node, pulled back on save Implements the contract through an adapter (QtGraphFrontend) directly on GraphView directly on ImGuiGraphView directly on BlenderGraphView

Pick the closest model and read it first. Retained/scene-based toolkits look like Qt; immediate-mode looks like ImGui; Flet sits between the two. If your host already has a node editor, read Blender — it is the case where the frontend supplies the seventeen verbs and draws nothing at all, which is the clearest illustration that the engine is not secretly shaped around a canvas.

docs.title: What you get for free
docs.text:
Everything in this list already works and must not be reimplemented.

Reading

  • read_graph(stage, context, chunks) — prims, ports and edges for one context.
  • contexts(stage) / default_context(stage) — which graphs a file holds, and which one to open. A file whose top level holds one chunkgroup is asking to be opened inside it; reading at CHUNKS_ROOT shows one node and none of the work.
  • [PortRef][usd_chunks.graph.engine.PortRef], iter_ports, param_port_type, sdf_to_port_type — ports and their typing.
  • node_position / graph_position / write_position — see Coordinates below.

Authoring

  • can_connect, connect, disconnect. Never author a connection yourself; connect also writes the @Node.param@ expression that makes a typed wire resolve.
  • create_from_entry(scene, entry, usd_pos, nest) — the create sequence, including the position hook and the narrow exception set. It returns (created, error).
  • paste_nodes(...) and rewire_pasted(...) — materialize a clipboard selection and re-wire it. rewire_pasted reads ports off the stage, so it works before a reload.
  • group_into_chunkgroup(...) — the whole group operation: read the boundary, snapshot, delete, make the group, paste inside, wire it back into the chain.
  • delete_chunks, toggle_disabled, collapse_or_expand, apply_selection, chunks_for.

Collapsed nodes

New nodes start collapsed (start_collapsed, which create_from_entry already calls), so a collapsed node has to be wireable without opening it:

  • is_collapsed(chunk) says whether to draw a node collapsed.
  • collapsed_node_ports(chunk, path, ports, edges) cuts a node's read_graph ports down to what it shows: its exec ports and the wired end of each wired param. It also says whether each side gets a "+".
  • A wire that ends on a "+" carries a PlusRef where a PortRef would be.
  • plus_step(chunks, a, b) says what to ask when either end of a wire is a "+": a list of params, and what the picked one then joins to.
  • param_menu_label labels each param in that list, e.g. "Translate › X".

Keep the pending pick in the view, and have a choose() that joins it. The menu should only show the pending pick; that way a test can drive the whole join without a window. Flet, ImGui and Blender all do it this way.

Clipboard

ClipboardNode, ClipboardEdge, and the module-level node_clipboard / edge_clipboard, via copy_to_clipboard(nodes, edges). These are shared between frontends — a selection copied in one can be pasted in another — so assign into the lists, never rebind them.

View slots

read_active_slot, write_active_slot, activate_view_slot, new_view_slot, default_view_slot, context_has_output, create_output_for. The active view drives execution while there is one: chunk_stage.recook_for_view cooks its upstream tree and blocks everything else. With no active view a context cooks to its Output, so a context with neither cooks nothing at all. Call default_view_slot when you open a graph: it gives a context with neither an Output (and returns no slot, so reload if the chunk count changed). Every non-Qt frontend once shipped without it and looked correct while doing nothing.

Navigation and layout

can_dive, parent_context, nest_target, menu_entries, exec_boundary, layout_adjacency, layout_graph, and the algorithm in chunk_graph_layout.

docs.title: What you must implement
docs.text:
[GraphFrontend][usd_chunks.graph.engine.GraphFrontend] names seventeen verbs:

set_selection      selected_chunks
delete_selected    toggle_disable_selected    collapse_selected_or_all
copy_selection     cut_selection      paste_at    duplicate_selection
group_selection    create_chunk
can_dive           dive_into          dive_out
active_slot        set_active_slot
frame
