It is a Protocol, not a base class, so there is nothing to inherit. Add your class to frontends() in tests/test_graph_frontend_contract.py on day one — the failures are your to-do list, and the test checks signatures as well as names.

Most of these are now three or four lines: call the engine, then save, reload and set a status. An engine function never reloads, never saves and never sets a status — it returns what you need in order to do those things the way your toolkit does them. If your implementation of a verb is thirty lines, check whether you are rewriting something above.

Drawing and input are deliberately not in the contract. They have no shared shape, and a test asserts they stay out.

docs.title: Coordinates
docs.text:
USD is Y-up. Most canvases are Y-down. graph_position(prim) returns canvas space and is the only correct way to read a node position for drawing; write_position(prim, x, y) takes the coordinates USD stores, so convert on the way in as you converted on the way out.

Blender is the exception that proves the rule: its node editor is Y-up like USD, so its frontend passes positions straight through — and consequently its duplicate_selection offsets by -40 where the others use +40. The conversion is yours; the authoring is not.

This is not a detail. The flip originally lived inside a private Qt helper, so the second frontend had no flip at all and rendered every file mirrored — a node dragged in one jumped to the other side when opened in the other.

docs.title: Six things that will bite you
docs.text:
1. Diving does not change where new chunks land. add_chunk parents to the scene's current context, which navigating does not set. Wrap creation in scene.creating_in(nest_target(...)), or a node created inside a group silently lands outside it — and on a brand-new network it lands in the scene's default chunkgroup, which is not the graph you are showing, so the create appears to do nothing at all.

2. Selection belongs on the chunk, not on your view. The shared operations read ChunkFlags.State.SELECTED. A selection kept privately is invisible to them, and copy_selection will find nothing. Use apply_selection, which writes the bit for you.

3. Passing the conformance test is not evidence of working. It checks that the verbs exist with the right signatures. Every frontend has shipped bugs it could never have caught: all of Flet's pointer handlers raised AttributeError on first touch while looking perfectly implemented, Qt's clipboard was not actually shared despite correct verbs, and Blender called a state method that does not exist, in two places, because the tests each asserted only the direction that happened to work. Write behavioural tests — see tests/test_qt_graph_frontend.py and tests/test_chunk_graph.py — and assert both directions of anything that toggles.

4. Catch narrowly. The clear_state bug above survived because it sat inside a bare except Exception. If you are guarding against "a chunk object that carries no state bits", catch AttributeError and let everything else surface.

5. Keyboard shortcuts collide with text entry. If your toolkit dispatches keys at the window level, a Delete meant for a text field will delete the selected node. Flet solves this with frontends.flet.factory.FocusTracker: widgets report focus, and the graph checks before acting. Qt does not need it because its widgets consume keys first, and Blender and ImGui do not because their editors own key routing.

6. dive_out may not exist in your toolkit's terms. Qt navigates by opening a tab, so "out" is a back-step through the docker's navigation history; the others swap the context in place. Same verb, genuinely different mechanism. Implement whichever your shell supports, and make it a documented no-op if it supports neither. Use parent_context to decide where out is — it walks up to a path that actually holds chunks, which a single rsplit does not.

docs.title: What is deliberately not shared
docs.text:
Qt's materialization. The three synchronous frontends share materialize and paste_nodes. Qt does not: it defers wiring a paste through a QTimer because its ports arrive in deferred proxy batches, guards a window with chunk._executing, and blocks pasted chunks when the context has an active view. Those steps are the difference, so a shared implementation would be one function with a Qt branch inside it. If your widgets appear asynchronously, copy Qt; if they appear immediately, call paste_nodes.

Applying a layout. layout_graph computes the positions for everyone. Applying them does not generalise: Blender must set both the node and the prim, ImGui must tell the editor because it owns positions from then on, and Flet writes its own dict.

Framing. Blender selects and calls bpy.ops.node.view_selected, ImGui calls navigate_to_content, Qt unions rects and calls fitInView, Flet solves a zoom and a pan by hand. There is nothing left in common once the toolkit has a viewport.

Node locking. Qt and Blender mark nodes whose prim comes from an external or referenced layer (the rule is the same in both: the strongest non-anonymous, non-root opinion is not the edit target) and pass is_locked to layout_graph so auto-layout routes around them. Qt refuses the drag; Blender cannot, so it drops the dragged position when writing back and the next reload restores it. Flet and ImGui have no such concept yet, so a layout there can move a node the other two would have pinned. If your frontend can express it, implement it.

Staying honest between reloads. A frontend whose toolkit owns the editing (Blender) must also catch what the toolkit does behind its back. Blender's frontend shadows the stock node operators (delete, duplicate, copy/paste, mute) with the chunk verbs inside its tree type, diffs the tree's links against the model's edges in NodeTree.update so a cut wire disconnects in USD, listens for chunk notices (value, state, param add/remove, delete, prim resync) and re-mirrors the touched nodes one tick later, and after every undo/redo puts the chunk prims back to the step Blender restored (addon/undo.py) and rebuilds from USD -- because Blender's undo restores the .blend, never the stage. Undo covers chunk prims only; see docs/undo.md. A canvas frontend gets all of this for free by being the only writer of its scene.

Node locking. Qt marks nodes whose prim comes from an external or referenced layer and refuses to move them during auto-layout. Blender does the same, dropping the drag on write-back since it cannot refuse one. Flet and ImGui have no such concept yet, so a layout there can move a node Qt would have pinned. If your frontend can express it, implement it. Dive keys on chunk_stage.is_subnet: a chunkgroup, or a chunk hosting a referenced network (a Reference, Sublayer or Payload pointed at a saved network file). A lock is about position, not params: a locked node's params are meant to be edited, and the edit lands as an over in the stage's edit target (chunk_utils.host_edit_layer), so a shot can tweak a sequence's network without touching the sequence file.

docs.title: Param widgets
docs.text:
A graph frontend also needs a widget per param type, which is a separate extension point with its own guide — see Plugins. Implement [ChunkWidgetFactoryBase][usd_chunks.chunk_widget_api.ChunkWidgetFactoryBase] and one [ChunkParamWidgetBase][usd_chunks.chunk_widget_api.ChunkParamWidgetBase] subclass per ChunkFlags.ParamType.

Cover every type in the factory map from the start. A Menu param crashed the Flet frontend on startup for a while because no test network happened to contain one, so that branch of the factory had never once executed. tests/test_flet_widgets.py shows the shape of the test that prevents it: build every widget the factory can return, from a real param.

Two typing traps, both found the hard way in Blender. A Slider declares INT and FLOAT — one class serves both, and is_int is what decides; testing the flags in the wrong order makes every float slider an integer one, and the symptom is a param that silently fails to mirror rather than an error. And containers (Vector, Group) hold the params you actually want: skipping anything without a get_type gives a node with a port for tz and no control for it.

docs.title: Houdini
docs.text:
In Houdini, every chunk is a LOP node in Solaris. You put chunks down from the Tab menu, wire them to each other and to any other LOP, and their params are normal Houdini parms.

You need Houdini 21.0 and a clone of usd_chunks. Tested with Houdini 21.0 on Windows.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
The commands below use C:\src\usd_chunks for the clone and Houdini 21.0.868. Change them to match yours.

Step 1. Clone usd_chunks:

git clone https://github.com/HuginStudios/usd_chunks.git C:\src\usd_chunks

Step 2. Install typing-extensions for Houdini:

"C:\Program Files\Side Effects Software\Houdini 21.0.868\python311\python.exe" -m pip install --target "%LOCALAPPDATA%\usd_chunks\installed_deps\py311" typing-extensions

Step 3. Point Houdini at the usd_chunks package:

setx HOUDINI_PACKAGE_DIR C:\src\usd_chunks\usd_chunks\hosts\houdini\packages

If HOUDINI_PACKAGE_DIR is already set, for V-Ray say, don't use setx. Add the folder to the end of it in Windows' Environment Variables window, after a ;.

Step 4. Start Houdini. Open a LOP network, such as /stage, press Tab and type mesh. Mesh shows up under usdchunks.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: git pull. Houdini reads usd_chunks straight from the clone, so there's nothing to reinstall. The same setup works for every Houdini version that runs Python 3.11.

docs.title: Using chunks in Houdini
docs.text:
• The Tab menu. All chunks are under usdchunks, sorted into categories like Modelling and Transform.
  • Houdini owns the graph. Chunks connect with normal LOP wires and cook when a parm or something upstream changes.
  • Params are Houdini parms. They take keys and expressions and save with the .hip. To read another chunk's param, use ch("../mesh1/radius").
  • Viewport handles. Select a chunk node and press Enter in the viewport. Its box gizmos become Houdini's bounding box handle: drag a face and only that face moves, so a Blockout Box's faces snap to its Snap step. Its translate gizmos become move handles. Drags undo like any Houdini handle. Other gizmo types (rotate, scale, transform, scalar, brush) have no handle in Houdini yet, so use the parms for those.
  • Networks travel between apps. Tab > usdchunks > Chunk Import... loads a network saved in usdview or Blender. A Chunkgroup node's Export Network... button writes one back.

The details, including what doesn't work in Houdini yet, are in the Houdini host README.

docs.title: If something is wrong
docs.text:
The Tab menu has no chunks. You only see Chunk and Chunkgroup, or nothing under usdchunks. usd_chunks didn't load. The Houdini console says why, in a line starting with usd_chunks: not loaded. The usual causes:

  • Step 3 didn't take. setx only reaches programs started after it, so start Houdini again from a new window.
  • Step 2 is missing. The console names typing_extensions.
  • houdini.env sets PYTHONPATH. A PYTHONPATH line in Documents\houdini21.0\houdini.env replaces the package's value. Remove the line, or add the clone to it: PYTHONPATH = C:/src/usd_chunks.
  • Another USD is on PYTHONPATH. A system-wide PYTHONPATH that points at a different USD build breaks Houdini's Python. Don't set PYTHONPATH system-wide.

Step 2 fails with a pip error. With no internet, or with a network that checks HTTPS traffic (it fails with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED), Houdini's pip can't reach PyPI. Run the same command with any other Python 3 that can.

A chunk is missing from the Tab menu. The chunk needs a pip package that isn't installed. When you put one down from the Tab menu, Houdini asks to install it. A .hip that loads never asks; the node shows an error until the package is installed. See If a chunk is missing from the menu.

usd_chunks loads twice. If you set it up the old way, with install.py, delete Documents\houdini21.0\packages\usd_chunks.json.

docs.title: Notes on the install
docs.text:
• Why Houdini's python311\python.exe? It's Houdini's own Python 3.11 without the Houdini parts, so it needs no licence. hython would also work, but needs a licence that can run it.
  • Why a separate folder for typing-extensions? Houdini's own Python is shared by every plugin and replaced on upgrade. usd_chunks looks in %LOCALAPPDATA%\usd_chunks\installed_deps\py311 by itself.
  • attrs is older than usd_chunks asks for. Houdini 21 ships attrs 22.2 and usd_chunks asks for 25.4 or newer. usd_chunks works with Houdini's copy, so leave it alone.
  • Don't install usd-core or the [standalone] extra for Houdini, and don't pip install usd_chunks into Houdini's Python. Houdini has its own USD.
  • Without the package. For a launcher of your own, set these before starting Houdini instead of step 3: HOUDINI_PATH to C:\src\usd_chunks\usd_chunks\hosts\houdini;& (keep the &, and quote the set line in cmd) and PYTHONPATH to C:\src\usd_chunks.
  • install.py is the old setup. It writes a package file into one Houdini version's packages folder instead.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
To get usd_chunks working, install the package into the Python your host runs. It comes with a set of chunks, so that's all you need to start. Set USD_CHUNK_DIRS later, when you write chunks of your own.

This page covers usdview and plain Python. Houdini and Blender install differently: see Houdini and Blender.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
You need Python 3.11+, and it has to be the same Python your USD was built with (see Requirements). On Windows, where python is usdview's own Python:

git clone https://github.com/HuginStudios/usd_chunks.git C:\src\usd_chunks
python -m pip install -e C:\src\usd_chunks
set PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME=C:\src\usd_chunks\usd_chunks\hosts\usdview
usdview anything.usda

The third line tells usdview where the usd_chunks plugin is: the usd_chunks\hosts\usdview folder inside your clone. In PowerShell, write it as $env:PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME = "C:\src\usd_chunks\usd_chunks\hosts\usdview". On macOS/Linux, use export PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME=/path/to/usd_chunks/usd_chunks/hosts/usdview.

set only lasts until you close that window. To keep it, put the line in the script you start usdview with.

If pip install -e fails, your pip is probably too old for editable installs. Run python -m pip install --upgrade pip and try again.

If pip fails with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED, your network checks HTTPS traffic and that pip is too old to use Windows' own certificates. Pip 24.2 and newer use them. Download a new pip with any Python that works (python -m pip download pip --no-deps -d wheels), then install that file with the old one (python -m pip install wheels\pip-<version>.whl).

To run without usdview, using usd-core only:

git clone https://github.com/HuginStudios/usd_chunks.git
python -m pip install -e "./usd_chunks[standalone]"
usdchunks run --help

For something to run, the Scripting page builds and saves a small network.

For other variables on this page, use $env:NAME = "value" in PowerShell and export NAME=value on macOS/Linux.

In usdview, right-click the graph canvas (or press Tab) to see the chunks in chunks/. When you start writing your own chunks, point USD_CHUNK_DIRS at your own folder. You only need the rest of this page if something goes wrong or you want more detail.

No Chunks panel when usdview opens? Usually usd_chunks was installed into a different Python than the one usdview uses. See If the Chunks panel is missing.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.11 or newer. usd_chunks uses typing.dataclass_transform, which was added in 3.11.
  • The same Python your USD was built with. USD's Python bindings only work with the Python version they were compiled for, so usd_chunks has to be installed into that Python: usdview's, Maya's mayapy, and so on. If your USD was built with a Python older than 3.11, you need to rebuild USD with 3.11 or newer first. Houdini and Blender have their own setup: see Houdini and Blender.

docs.title: Getting the package
docs.text:
usd_chunks isn't on PyPI yet, so start by cloning it:

git clone https://github.com/HuginStudios/usd_chunks.git

How you install it depends on whether the Python you're installing into already has USD. Check with:

python -c "import pxr"

If that works, you're in usdview's Python, Maya's mayapy or another app that has USD. Install it as is:

python -m pip install -e ./usd_chunks

If that fails, you're in a plain Python (a script, a CI job, a new venv) and need USD as well:

python -m pip install -e "./usd_chunks[standalone]"

The standalone extra installs usd-core, so you get the library and the usdchunks command without building USD yourself. usdchunks run my_setup.usda works straight away.

🚫 Never install [standalone] into a host that already has USD

Houdini, Maya, Blender and usdview each ship their own USD build. Blender's, for example, is compiled as pxrBlender_v26_03__pxrReserved__. A second USD installed with pip is a completely separate library that can't share objects with the host's. You end up with two USDs in one process, and things break in confusing ways.

The usd-core package on PyPI doesn't include usdview. To use usd_chunks in usdview you need a full USD build that includes pxr.Usdviewq. Build one with OpenUSD's build_scripts/build_usd.py, or use a prebuilt one, such as NVIDIA's. See usdview integration below.

docs.title: ⚠️ A plain install won't show every bundled chunk
docs.text:
Warning

A plain install only includes attrs. About one in six of the chunks in chunks/ need another package, mostly numpy.

If a chunk module fails to import, it's left out of the create menu. The console shows a warning that names the missing package, then the import error. Nothing shows in the UI. Usually the first thing you notice is that the chunk you want isn't in the menu.

The chunks affected today: AMDMaterialXLibrary, add_curves, cad_import, curves_to_mesh, custom_widget, mesh, poly_reduce, rbd_solver, requirements (an example), scatter_brush, scatter_points, urdf_import, uv_checker and vine. That includes some of the main ones, like Mesh, Scatter, Poly Reduce and the RBD solver.

There are two ways to fix it:

  • Install the packages yourself: pip install numpy requests mujoco fast-simplification. mujoco is only for the RBD solver, and fast-simplification only for Poly Reduce. CAD Import also needs cadquery-ocp. Add PySide6 only if your host doesn't have Qt already; usdview, Houdini and Maya do. You can also install just the ones you need.
  • Let usd_chunks ask. When you create a chunk whose requirements (Writing a chunk) aren't installed, usdview asks "OK to install requests for chunk AMDMaterialXLibrary?" and installs them if you say yes, with a progress dialog. usdchunks run asks the same on an interactive terminal, and Blender in a popup.

docs.title: Other extras
docs.text:
These are only needed for specific work. You can combine them, for example pip install -e ".[dev,docs]".

Extra What it's for ui Installs PySide6, for a host that doesn't have Qt. usdview and Houdini already have Qt, so skip it there. flet Running the standalone Flet graph frontend (python -m usd_chunks.frontends.flet.nodegraph <network.usda>) instead of a Qt host. imgui The same for the Dear ImGui frontend (python -m usd_chunks.frontends.imgui.nodegraph <network.usda>). dev Working on usd_chunks itself: pytest, ruff, build tools, usd-core, and the Flet and ImGui frontends so the tests can cover them. docs Building the docs site. See Build documentation.

docs.title: usdview integration
docs.text:
usdview loads usd_chunks as a USD plugin, so it needs to know where the plugin's plugInfo.json is. You tell it with PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME.

For a clone, the path is the usd_chunks\hosts\usdview folder inside it, as in the quick start. If you installed another way, print the path with the same Python you installed into:

python -m usd_chunks.cli plugin-path

Set PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME to that path before starting usdview. With that and USD_CHUNK_DIRS set, usdview opens with a Chunks panel and a Chunks menu.

docs.title: If the Chunks panel is missing
⚠️ Installed into the wrong Python
docs.text:
This is the most common cause, and there's no error message: the panel just isn't there. Most machines have several Pythons installed, and usdview usually has its own, which is often not the one plain pip installs into.

Find out which Python usdview uses (run import sys; print(sys.executable) in its Python console, or look in your launcher script), then run pip with that Python:

"<that path>" -m pip install -e usd_chunks     # usdview
mayapy -m pip install -e usd_chunks            # Maya

Houdini and Blender don't use pip install like this. See Houdini and Blender.

If you already installed into the wrong Python, reinstall with the right one. A regular install can be fixed by pointing PYTHONPATH at that environment's site-packages, but an editable (-e) install can't. Editable installs rely on a .pth file, and Python only reads those from real site directories, not from PYTHONPATH.

docs.title: ⚠️ Testing the import from the folder you cloned into
docs.text: If you run python -c "..." or a script from the folder that contains usd_chunks/, Python imports that folder instead of your install. The error then names something odd, like ATTRS_VERSION, instead of saying the module wasn't found. Change to any other folder before testing with plain python. usdview and the usdchunks command aren't affected.

docs.title: If "usdchunks" is not recognized
docs.text:
pip put the usdchunks command in the Scripts folder of the Python you installed into, and that folder isn't on PATH. This is normal for usdview's own Python. Use python -m usd_chunks.cli instead, with that same Python. It takes the same commands:

python -m usd_chunks.cli run box_network.usda

Or add that Python's Scripts folder to PATH.

docs.title: If a chunk is missing from the menu
docs.text:
The panel is there, but a chunk like Scatter, Mesh or the RBD solver isn't in the create menu. This is almost always a missing pip package: the chunk failed to import, so it was left out. The console shows which package when it loads:

WARNING: usd_chunks.chunk_registry: Chunk scatter needs numpy>=2,<3, which is not installed. ...

Install that package into the Python usdview uses. The full list and the fix are under A plain install won't show every bundled chunk.

usdchunks list prints every chunk that was found, from the same USD_CHUNK_DIRS, so you can check outside usdview whether a chunk loads.

docs.title: Gizmos (viewport handles)
docs.text:
This section is for usdview. Blender's add-on has its own handles, with nothing extra to install (see Blender). Houdini has none yet.

In usdview, the handles you drag in the viewport to change a chunk's params are in a separate repo, usd_gizmos. Once usd_chunks is set up, it takes three more commands:

git clone https://github.com/HuginStudios/usd_gizmos.git
"<usdview's python>" -m pip install -e ./usd_gizmos
set PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME=%PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME%;C:\path\to\usd_gizmos\gizmo\plugins\usdview

PowerShell: $env:PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME += ";C:\path\to\usd_gizmos\gizmo\plugins\usdview". macOS/Linux: export PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME="$PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME:/path/to/usd_gizmos/gizmo/plugins/usdview".

As with usd_chunks, install it with usdview's own Python (see Installed into the wrong Python). The path ends in ...\plugins\usdview. The folder next to it, ...\plugins\kraken, is for Kraken and easy to pick by mistake.

What you should see: select any prim and a transform handle appears in the viewport. When you drag it, a Transform chunk appears in the graph and stores the move. Dragging never changes the prim directly. Camera and Scatter Brush chunks have their own handles.

docs.title: How the two repos split the work
docs.text: usd_chunks only describes a handle. A chunk lists gizmos in its config() (Writing a chunk), which writes ui:gizmo:* attributes saying which handle exists and which params it controls. usd_gizmos draws the handle and handles the dragging. Each repo works without the other: without usd_gizmos you just don't see handles, and without usd_chunks the handles don't control any chunk params. See Chunk gizmos: the host contract if you're building handles for another host.

docs.title: If the handle is missing, or dragging doesn't change the params
docs.text:
• No handle at all: PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME doesn't include usd_gizmos\gizmo\plugins\usdview (make sure you didn't pick the kraken folder), or usd_gizmos was installed into a different Python than usdview's.
  • A handle shows, but the chunk's params don't change: an older gizmo plugin is loaded as well. Both replace the same viewport functions, and nothing on screen shows which one you're using. This usually happens in one of two ways:
    • A usdview bundle that includes its own copy (for example usdviewTools\gizmo), loaded because the whole usdviewTools folder is on the plugin path. List only the subfolders you want.

    • A saved user-level PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME that points at an old plugins folder. Any launcher that adds to the variable picks it up. Check it with:

      [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME", "User")

docs.title: Running from a clone
docs.text:
If you want to run from a checkout of this repo without installing it (for example while working on usd_chunks itself), add the repo root to PYTHONPATH so usdview's Python can import the usd_chunks package:

set PYTHONPATH=C:\path\to\usd_chunks;%PYTHONPATH%

You still need PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME. Without an install there's no usdchunks command, so get the path with python -m usd_chunks.cli plugin-path instead.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Default What it does USD_CHUNK_DIRS the bundled chunks The folders your chunk modules are in, separated by ; on Windows and : on macOS/Linux. Each folder is searched, including subfolders, for .py files with a main() function. See Writing a chunk. If two folders have a chunk with the same name, the one in the first folder is used. A ready-made set of chunks ships with usd_chunks (the repository's chunks/ folder) and is always searched after the folders you list, so yours win on a duplicate name. USD_CHUNK_DEPENDENCY_DIR %LOCALAPPDATA%/usd_chunks/installed_deps (~/.cache/... elsewhere) Where the pip packages a chunk needs are installed, in a py<version> subfolder per Python (usdview and Blender run different ones). It's added to sys.path automatically. USD_CHUNK_AUTO_INSTALL unset (ask) What happens when a chunk's requirements (Writing a chunk) aren't installed. Unset: ask once per chunk ("OK to install requests for chunk AMDMaterialXLibrary?") -- usdview in a dialog, usdchunks run on an interactive terminal, Blender in a popup (with Allow Online Access on); a yes installs into USD_CHUNK_DEPENDENCY_DIR with progress shown, and a "no" stands until restart. CI and other non-interactive runs only warn. 1: install without asking (Blender installs in the background, with progress in the status bar, and recooks the chunks after). 0: never install, only warn. USD_CHUNK_LOAD_FILTER (unset, so everything loads) Only load the chunk modules you list, for example USD_CHUNK_LOAD_FILTER=transform,scatter_points. A module loads if its name appears anywhere in the string, so transform also lets a module called trans load, but not one called transform_ops. Useful for a quick test with only a few chunks loaded. USD_CHUNK_VERBOSE off When two chunk modules have the same name, the first USD_CHUNK_DIRS folder wins and the log only gets a one-line summary. Set this to log every clash, with the file that was used and the one that was skipped. PXR_PLUGINPATH_NAME — Only needed for usdview. See usdview integration. PYTHONPATH — Only needed when running from a clone instead of an install. See Running from a clone. USD_CHUNK_LOG_LEVEL INFO usd_chunks' own log level: DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR or CRITICAL. Any other value is treated as INFO. Set it to DEBUG to see what a reload or cook does, param by param. That includes why a config() fell back to defaults, which is otherwise only a log line. The CLI, usdview, Blender and the graph frontends print these to the console; a script of your own calls usd_chunks.configure_logging() to do the same. USD_CHUNKS_COOK_CACHE on For chunks whose module sets cache_cook. =0 never reads or writes the cache, =refresh cooks every time and rewrites what is stored. USD_CHUNKS_OPEN_CACHE on Saving a network also keeps each chunk's result in the cook cache folder, and opening it reads them back instead of cooking, while nothing a chunk depends on has changed (see Opening without cooking). =0 always cooks on open. USD_CHUNKS_COOK_CACHE=0 turns this off too, and =refresh keeps storing but never reads back. USD_CHUNKS_COOK_CACHE_DIR %LOCALAPPDATA%/usd_chunks/cook_cache (~/.cache/usd_chunks/cook_cache elsewhere) Where cached cooks are kept. Safe to delete at any time. USD_CHUNKS_COOK_CACHE_MAX_GB 2 The most the cook cache may use. Each time something is stored, results unread for 30 days are deleted, then the least recently read until the folder fits. USD_CHUNKS_PROBE_DELEGATES (auto-detected) Whether to ask render delegates for their settings. In a GUI host like usdview (when a QApplication is running) they are asked by a separate Python process, because loading a second render engine in the host can crash it; the answer is cached on disk. Scripts and tests ask in their own process. =1 always asks in-process, =0 never asks. Note the name starts with USD_CHUNKS_, unlike the other variables. USD_CHUNKS_TIMINGS off =1 times every chunk's cook, and its commit (where a chunk writes a file or renders, so a Render chunk's time is there). Each one is logged as it finishes, with its own time (less any cook started inside it, such as an upstream chunk it cooked first). usdchunks run also prints a summary at the end: how long opening, loading and cooking took, and the slowest chunks first. usdchunks run --timings does the same for one run. USD_CHUNKS_START_COLLAPSED on Nodes you create in the graph start collapsed, showing only their header and wired ports; double-click one to open it. =0 starts them open. Nodes in a file you open keep however they were saved.

docs.title: Build documentation
docs.text:
The reference pages are generated from the source code, so usd_chunks has to be importable when you build. Install the docs extra and build:

pip install -e ".[docs]"
set USD_CHUNK_DIRS=chunks
mkdocs serve

mkdocs serve runs the site locally, and mkdocs build writes it to site/ instead.

Each release's docs are published to https://huginstudios.github.io/usd_chunks/ when its tag is pushed (see "Making a release" in CONTRIBUTING.md). CI doesn't build the docs on pull requests, so if something is broken you'll find out when you publish.

On Windows, build_docs.bat does both. With no arguments it runs the site locally. With --share it builds the site and copies it to a folder you choose, such as a network share, a mapped drive or a web server folder:

build_docs.bat --share \\server\share\usd_chunks_docs
build_docs.bat --share E:\www\usd_chunks --directory-urls

It adds and overwrites files but never deletes them. Add --mirror to also delete files that are no longer part of the site. That only works if the destination is empty or was published by this script before, and publishing into something that looks like a source checkout is always refused.

By default it builds plain file names (example.html), which work both from a file share and from a web server. A browser opening files from a share won't turn /example/ into /example/index.html, so the default mkdocs URLs would break there. If the site is served by a web server such as nginx, you can pass --directory-urls for cleaner URLs.

Search only works when the site is served over http, because browsers block the search index from loading over file://. Everything else works from a plain file share.

Run docs/gen_ref_nav.py to regenerate the docs/reference markdown files.

docs.title: 🚀 Your first chunk node
docs.text:
1. Open usdview. The graph is the Graph tab in the Chunks panel.
  2. Right-click the empty canvas and pick a chunk, for example Mesh. If the graph has no View yet, one is added and connected for you.
  3. Change the node's params in its panel and watch the viewport update.
  4. To see the output of another chunk you add later, right-click it and choose Set View. A View is only added for you when the graph has none.

That's all you need for a working chunk. The rest of this page covers connecting several nodes, keyboard shortcuts, disabled and locked nodes, and working inside a ChunkGroup. For how the graph is stored (prims, ports, USD connections), see The graph is USD. For more on Output, View and ChunkGroup, see Output, View and ChunkGroup.

docs.title: Opening the graph
docs.text: The Graph tab shows the graph you're currently in: the top level, or the inside of a ChunkGroup if you're in one. Each graph remembers which of its views was active when you saved, and opens on that one.

docs.title: The Params page
docs.text:
The Params tab next to it has two boxes.

  • The group's box, at the top, is the graph's interface: the params and the chunks lofted to it (see ChunkGroup). To put a chunk there, right-click it and choose Loft up chunk. A chunk made from the Params tab's own create menu is lofted for you, so it shows where you made it. Click the box's title to fold it.
  • The search box, below it, finds any other chunk in the graph. Type in it and it shows the chunks that match and aren't lofted. The line under the search bar says how many it found, and how many lofted chunks above match too. Searching never changes the group's box.

docs.title: Creating a node
docs.text:
Right-click the empty canvas to open the create menu. Chunks are sorted by the category set in each module's config() (see Writing a chunk). Pick one and it's added at the cursor.

If you drag a wire out of any port, input or output, and let go on empty canvas, the same menu opens. The chunk you pick is created and connected to the port you dragged from. The menu isn't filtered, so you can pick a chunk with no matching port. In that case the node is created without a wire, and no error is shown.

To build a chain quickly, tick Auto-connect in the bottom-right corner, next to the Output badge. Each chunk you then make from the create menu is wired after the selected node. With no node selected, or several, it goes after the one the active Output or View shows. The Output or View moves onto the new chunk, and the new chunk is selected, so the next one goes after it. The box is remembered between sessions.

A node's header shows its icon, name and type (to set an icon, see Icons in the node graph). The ⋮ button at its right opens the same menu as right-clicking the node.

To make a node wider or narrower, drag its right edge. Double-click the edge to go back to the default width. The width is saved in the file, on the chunk prim's ui:nodegraph:node:size.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Drag from one port to another port of the same type to connect them. A port lights up when the mouse comes near it, to show you can start a wire there. A port's colour always shows its type of value.

While you drag, the ports you can drop on get a white ring. Near one, the end of the wire jumps onto it, turns solid, and the port lights up: that's where the wire lands if you let go. Away from any port, the end follows the mouse again, dashed.

A few things work differently:

  • Drop a node onto an exec wire to insert it. The exec wire is the chain wire between outputs:chunk and inputs:chunk. It's split and goes through the node.
  • Shake a node quickly back and forth to disconnect all its wires. The exec chain is joined back up behind it: whatever fed the node now feeds what the node used to feed, so taking a step out of the middle doesn't break the rest. Value wires are just removed.
  • Connecting a value port writes a real @Node.param@ expression, so it's an actual data connection, not just a line on screen (see The graph is USD and Expressions).

docs.title: Nothing cooks without an Output or a View
docs.text:
Only chunks connected to the active View cook, or with no active View, the ones connected to the graph's Output. A new chain does nothing until it's connected to one. Right-click the chunk whose output you want to see and choose Set View 2 or Set View 3. That connects that View to the chunk's output (creating it if needed) and makes it active. The slot already looking at the chunk is shown ticked. Until then, the nodes are set up but don't run. This is on purpose, not a bug.

A graph can have up to two views, numbered 2 and 3. Press 2 or 3 to switch to one, and 1 to go back to the Output. To end the graph at another chunk, right-click it and choose Set Output. A key only switches to something the current graph has, so you can't blank the graph by accident.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
Key Does F Frame the selection (or everything, if nothing is selected). Ctrl+F Find a node by name or chunk type (untick Name or Type to search only the other). Enter frames the best match; Ctrl+Enter frames the next one each press. 1 Cook to the Output. 2 / 3 Switch to that view, if it exists. L Auto-layout the selection, or the whole graph if nothing is selected. With a backdrop selected, only the nodes inside it. B Put a backdrop around the selection (or at the cursor, if nothing is selected). N Add a sticky note at the cursor. C Collapse the selection, or the whole graph if nothing is selected. D Disable or enable the selection. Delete Delete the selection, backdrops and notes included. A deleted backdrop leaves its nodes where they are. Esc Cancel a wire drag, or clear focus. Tab Open the create menu at the cursor. Ctrl+C / Ctrl+X / Ctrl+V Copy / cut / paste the selection. A selected backdrop comes with everything in it. Ctrl+D Duplicate the selection. A duplicated backdrop goes just below the original. Ctrl+G Put the selection into a new ChunkGroup. A selected backdrop goes in with everything in it.

Some keys do one thing on their own and another with Ctrl (D/Ctrl+D, C/Ctrl+C). The plain key is the graph action, and the Ctrl version is the usual clipboard action.

docs.title: Backdrops and sticky notes
docs.text:
A backdrop is a coloured box that frames part of the network. Select some nodes and press B to put one around them. Drag its title bar or its edge and every node inside moves with it. A node counts as inside when the middle of its title bar is in the box. Drag the bottom-right corner to resize it. Clicking or dragging in the middle of a backdrop still does what it does on the empty canvas: box-select, or right-click to add a chunk.

A sticky note says what a part of the network is for. Press N to add one at the cursor, then type. Drag it anywhere on its body.

Both are also in the chunk menu (Tab or right-click on the canvas), at the bottom, and you can search for them there.

Double-click either one to edit its text. Right-click its title bar (or anywhere on a note) to change its colour, fit a backdrop around its nodes, lay out the nodes inside it, cut, copy, duplicate, put it in a ChunkGroup, or delete it. Select a backdrop and press L to lay out only the nodes inside it. Wires to nodes outside the box are ignored. A plain L keeps every backdrop whole: its nodes are laid out inside it, and the box moves as one block, with its notes.

Cut, copy, duplicate and Ctrl+G on a selected backdrop take everything in it: its nodes, and the backdrops and notes inside it. Delete removes only the backdrop and leaves its nodes where they are.

Both are saved in the scene as USD Backdrop prims next to the chunks. Undo covers them too. Scripts can make and change them: see Scripting.

docs.title: Which chunk made this prim?
docs.text:
Select a prim in the viewport and the graph shows which chunks it came from:

  • The chunk that made it gets a gold ring tagged made.
  • Each chunk that changed it (moved it, bound a material, set a property) gets a teal ring with a number: 1 changes it first, and the highest number wins a value they both set.
  • A prim inside an asset that a chunk referenced in (a mesh inside a Reference chunk's asset) has no chunk of its own. The chunk that brought it in gets a lavender ring.

A chunk inside a ChunkGroup you're not looking into rings the group's node. The line at the bottom of the graph says the same in words, for example /World/house/walls ← made by House · changed by Transform3, Paint. Click a name to jump to that node, or frame them to fit them all in view. Select several prims and the graph rings every chunk that made or changed any of them.

The other way round, right-click a node and pick Select Its Prims. The viewport selects what that chunk made (the outermost prim it made, such as /World/house, not every board) and each prim it changed.

None of this slows a big scene down. It's worked out from the selected prims' own layers, only when the selection changes, and nothing happens while you cook or orbit.

docs.title: Disabled and locked nodes
docs.text:
A disabled chunk (D) stays on the canvas, greyed out, so you can turn it back on. It doesn't cook or produce output.

A locked node comes from a layer you don't own, such as a ChunkGroup loaded as a reference, sublayer or payload. It has an amber header and can't be moved, not even by auto-layout, which works around it. You can still edit its params. Your edits are written as an over in your own edit target, so a shot can change a shared sequence's params without changing the sequence file.

docs.title: Going inside a ChunkGroup
docs.text: Double-click a ChunkGroup node to go inside and work on its contents as a separate graph, with its own views. New chunks you create while inside a group are added to that group. See ChunkGroup for how params are shared with the outside (lofting).

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: Plugins refer to implementations of usd_chunks for specific applications. For example, UsdView can use the chunks with the chunk_usdview plugin. Any plugin may want to provide a ui 'plugin' as well, that can translate the chunks to specific ui frameworks. At the moment, the repository contains a plugin for Qt, but as the library is build with interpopability in mind, we aim to support more ui frameworks in the future.

docs.title: Implementing a UI plugin
docs.text:
Although the chunks works as-is with USD, a major benefit of the chunks are that they can easily be represented in graphically. The initial idea of the library was to have a simple way for users to create plugin for Usdview, without having to create actual plugins. The chunks themselves are, simply put, containers of data with connections to and from said data. Any modification to the data will send a notice, and any listener may react to the notices. This makes implementing a ui framework on top of the chunks straight-forward, as the ui framework just need to implement the widget logic and listen to some notices.

There are some chunk-specifics though that will need to be considered when implementing an external ui framework.

docs.title: ChunkParamWidget
docs.text:
Firstly, all 'widgets' representing a valued parameter (params subclassed from ChunkParamBase), should subclass chunk_widget_api.ChunkParamWidgetBase. This class provide some basic param<->widget communication, meaning setters and getters of the parameter. Here's an example for taken from chunk_qt, implementing the chunk.Splinbox parameter:

class ChunkFloatSpinboxWidget(ChunkParamWidgetBase[chunk.Spinbox], QtWidgets.QDoubleSpinBox):
    def __init__(self, param: chunk.Spinbox):
        super().__init__(param)

        self._step = 1

        min_val = param.min_value
        max_val = param.max_value

        if min_val is not None:
            self.setMinimum(min_val * self._step)

        if max_val is not None:
            self.setMaximum(max_val * self._step)

        self.setup_chunk_widget()
        self.valueChanged.connect(self.value_changed)

    def get_value(self):
        return self.value()

    def set_value(self, value):
        return self.setValue(value)

    def wheelEvent(self, event: QtGui.QWheelEvent):
        event.ignore()

the setup_chunk_widget() function is implemented by [ChunkParamWidgetBase][usd_chunks.chunk_widget_api.ChunkParamWidgetBase] and will call set_value(), set_label(), set_icon() and set_set_param_layout() respectively, each with the corresponding arguments taken from the param.

The get_* and set_* functions of a ChunkParamWidgetBase should set/get the value of the ui widget only. Any changes to the value of the widget should trigger value_changed() of ChunkParamWidgetBase. The value_changed() function is concrete and responsible for setting the value back to the actual parameter.

The handle to the chunk param is a weakref.ref() object, meaning it may be set to None in case the param has been deleted. Hence, it's advised to check if the param is None prior to doing anything with it.

docs.title: ChunkWidgetFactoryBase
docs.text:
A ui implementation may want to create a subclass of [ChunkWidgetFactoryBase][usd_chunks.chunk_widget_api.ChunkWidgetFactoryBase] for mapping various params to their respective ui widgets. An example from chunk_qt: 

class ChunkQTWidgetFactory(chunk_widget_api.ChunkWidgetFactoryBase):
    widget_map: Dict[ChunkFlags.ParamType, type[QtWidgets.QWidget]] = {
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.FLOAT_SLIDER: ChunkSliderWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.INT_SLIDER: ChunkSliderWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.FLOAT_SPINBOX: ChunkFloatSpinboxWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.INT_SPINBOX: ChunkIntSpinboxWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.LABEL: ChunkLabelWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.LINEEDIT: ChunkLineEditWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.FILE: ChunkFileWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.STRING_MENU: ChunkComboBoxWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.CHECKBOX: ChunkCheckBoxWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.BUTTON: ChunkPushButtonWidget,
        ChunkFlags.ParamType.SEPARATOR: ChunkSeparatorWidget,
    }

    def create_widget(self, param: chunk.ChunkParamBase) -> ChunkParamWidget | None:
        """Create a Qt widget based on the ChunkParam object. The param.get_type() should determine the type of Qt Widget to create

        Args:
            param (chunk.ChunkParamBase): The parameter. The widget will update param.value when widget value is changed

        Returns:
            QtWidgets.QWidget: The QtWidget created
            None: If failed to create a widget
        """
        key = param.evaluate_type()
        widget_class = self.get_map().get(key, None)

        if not widget_class:
            logger.warning("Could not create widget for param %s: missing mapping in Qt factory", param.name)
            return None

        widget: ChunkParamWidget = widget_class(param)

        if param.tooltip and isinstance(widget, QtWidgets.QWidget):
            widget.setToolTip(param.tooltip)

        return widget

Using this (or any other factory if you prefer), enables easy creation of the widgets from params: 

widget = self.factory.create_widget(param)

A chunk Group parameter have an optional widget_factory member, that can dictate which widget_factory to use. For example, if a chunk group wishes to have special widgets for it's parameters, the ui plugin should respect this.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: All chunk objects (chunks, groups, params) are dynamic, meaning they may be created or deleted at runtime. This should be taken in to consideration when implementing a ui plugin. The notice system can help with this, as relevant creation / deletion notices are sent whenever a chunk object should be added or removed from the ui.

docs.title: ChunkContainerWidgetBase
docs.text: Similarly to the ChunkParamWidget, group widget classes can subclass the abstract ChunkContainerWidgetBase class which provides default implementations for much of the chunk->widget communication. However, any ui library specific functionality need be implemented by the ui plugin. See the chunk_qt ContainerWidget for an example.

docs.title: CHUNK_LOADED
docs.text:
A ui implementation may listen to the creation of chunks using the CHUNK_LOADED notice. When received, the ui implementation should create the chunk and all its parameters.

The ChunkWidgetDocker of the chunk_qt plugin listen to this notice, and will create the chunk widgets whenever the notice is received. A similar implementation may be relevant in other ui plugins as well.

docs.title: Application plugins
docs.text:
Host entry points live in usd_chunks.hosts: a plugin for Usdview, and one for Houdini Solaris, where every chunk is a LOP with native parms and Houdini owns the wiring (see Houdini).

Application plugins will vary in their implementations as the applications will load plugins differently. In some cases an application plugin may not be necessary at all.

In any case, using the chunks for any application require some initialization from the chunk_registry module. In the Usdview plugin, we do this inside of the ChunksPluginContainer.

...
    scene = UsdviewScene(usdviewApi)

    chunk_qt.build_chunk_docker(usdviewApi.qMainWindow)
    chunk_registry.ChunkLayerManager().initialize(usdviewApi.stage)
    chunk_registry.ChunkRegistry().initialize(scene, "chunk_usdview")

The UsdviewScene is an implementation of the abstract [SceneSender][usd_chunks.chunk_scene.SceneSender] class, which provides access to the scene as well as sends notices upon selection changes. Any application plugin should provide a similar scene proxy. This is important as some chunks will rely on prim selections, or other scene specific functionality. The scene proxy also provide a handle to the UsdStage, which the underlying application usually provides.

The ChunkRegistry is responsible for finding and loading any chunks in the environment, and the ChunkLayerManager is responsible for managing the SdfLayers of the chunks. Both of these need to be initialized in order to get proper functionality

In the case of the usdview plugin, we can use the chunk_qt ui plugin, as usdview uses Qt as well. This is expressed simply by calling the chunk_qt.build_chunk_docker function (chunk_qt being usd_chunks.frontends.qt.factory). For other applications not using Qt, an additional ui plugin would be needed to get the param widgets

docs.title: Building a chunk at runtime
docs.text:
A chunk doesn't have to come from a file. You can build one in Python (usdview's Python panel, a script, or a DCC's shell) and add it to the scene:

from usd_chunks import chunk

s = chunk.get_scene()
c = chunk.Chunk("hello")
s.add_chunk(c)
c.add_param(chunk.Slider("slider"))

The chunk shows up in the graph straight away, and you can connect it and use its params like any other chunk. It's the quickest way to try an idea before writing a module.

docs.title: What a save keeps
docs.text:
A chunk without its own module is saved as the runtime type. When you reopen the file, its name, params, values, wiring and position come back. The params are rebuilt from the attributes on its prim, so this is still there after reopening:

c.add_param(chunk.Slider("slider"))   # still there next time

Behaviour isn't saved. Callbacks are Python objects that only exist in the session that made them, and a saved file doesn't store them. A runtime chunk comes back with its params and data only. To make it do something again, you have to run its code again.

Also, an attribute only stores a param's type and value, not which widget it was. A float Slider comes back as the default widget for a float, without its range or label. Names, values and wiring come back exactly.

When a chunk is worth keeping, move it into a .py file in USD_CHUNK_DIRS with a main() that builds it. Then its behaviour comes back too, because the code is loaded from the file. See Writing a chunk.

docs.title: Scripting
docs.text:
You can build a network from Python instead of the node graph. A script makes the same chunks the graph does. What it builds opens as a graph, and a script can add to a graph you already have.

The short version, with the common jobs in one table, is the build-network skill: skills/usd-chunks-build-network/SKILL.md in the repository. This page is the full reference.

docs.title: In usdview
docs.text:
Open the Python interpreter (Window > Interpreter) and paste this:

from usd_chunks import Scene

with Scene.current() as scene:
    box = scene.create.cube(prim_path="/geo/box", width=2.0)
    scene.create.transform(box, primpath_location=box.get_param("prim_path"), ty=3.0)

The box shows up in the viewport, and the nodes show up in the graph. There is nothing to set up: if the Chunks panel works, this works too.

docs.title: In a terminal
docs.text:
Before you run a script, you need a Python with USD and usd_chunks installed in it. Use usdview's own Python, or install usd_chunks with python -m pip install -e "./usd_chunks[standalone]", which adds usd-core. See Install.

The chunks that come with usd_chunks are found by themselves. To use your own chunks too, set USD_CHUNK_DIRS to their folders, the same as for usdview.

Save this as box.py:

from usd_chunks import Scene

with Scene.new() as scene:
    box = scene.create.cube(prim_path="/geo/box", width=2.0)
    scene.create.transform(box, primpath_location=box.get_param("prim_path"), ty=3.0)

    scene.save("box_network.usda")   # the network: opens as a graph
    scene.export("box.usda")         # the result: plain USD, no Chunk prims

Then run it:

python box.py

Use Scene.current() in usdview and Scene.new() in a script. See Get a scene.

docs.title: Get a scene
docs.text:
Call Gives you Scene.new() A new, empty scene of your own. Scene.open(path) A saved network, loaded and cooked. Scene.current() The scene that is running now, such as usdview's. None if there is none.
  • Scene() is the same as Scene.new().
  • Scene(stage) works on a stage you already have.
  • A scene from Scene.new() is in metres (metersPerUnit 1). A Stage Settings chunk sets other units; a stage you pass in, or a network you open, keeps its own.
  • Only one scene can be live at a time. Leaving the with block closes a scene from Scene.new() or Scene.open(). Without with, call scene.close() when you are done.
  • Inside usdview, Scene.new() and Scene.open() raise an error. Use Scene.current().

docs.title: Make chunks
docs.text:
scene.create has one function per chunk:

  • Every chunk module, by its file name. transform.py is scene.create.transform(). Your own chunks in USD_CHUNK_DIRS work the same way.
  • Every menu entry, by its label in snake_case. Mesh's "Cube" entry is scene.create.cube(). Light's "Rect Light" is scene.create.rect_light().

Each function returns the chunk it made.

scene.create.transform(
    box,                                          # input: box runs first
    name="Lift",                                  # node name (optional)
    primpath_location=box.get_param("prim_path"), # a param: wired to follow it
    ty=3.0,                                       # a value: set
)

To find what you can make and set:

To see Use Every chunk you can make usdchunks list (or usdchunks list <word>), or dir(scene.create) What a chunk is for, and every param it takes usdchunks show transform, or help(scene.create.transform) A chunk's param names usdchunks show transform, or [p.name for p in chunk.get_params()] (group names are in the list too) Every chunk, in the order it was made scene.chunks_in_order() (scene.get_chunks() lists the newest first)

If the chunk name is in a string, use scene.add("transform", box, ty=3.0). This also works for a file name that is not a Python name, like my-node.py.

If a module and a menu entry have the same name, you get the module. If two menu entries have the same label, neither is in scene.create. Make the module and set its params instead.

docs.title: Set params
docs.text:
Pass params by name when you make the chunk. Params inside groups are found by name too.

lift = scene.create.transform(box, ty=3.0)

To change them later:

scene.set(lift, ty=5.0)
lift.get_param("ty").value = 5.0     # the same thing

Chunks cook again by themselves when a value changes.

A list param (Sublayer's imports, Scatter Points' prototypes) holds rows. Give it a Python list, one item per row. A dict sets a row's params by name, and the ones left out take their defaults. Where a row holds one param, the item can be just its value:

sets = scene.create.sublayer(imports=["lighting.usda", "set.usda"])   # first is strongest
rocks = scene.create.scatter_points(prototypes=[
    {"proto_path": "/assets/rock", "proto_weight": 200.0},
    {"proto_path": "/assets/bush"},
])

The list then has exactly those rows: setting it again with scene.set replaces them all. To change one param of one row and leave the rest, name it list.row.param. A list with fewer rows grows to hold the row you name:

scene.set(rocks, **{"prototypes.1.proto_weight": 50.0})
scene.set(sets, **{"imports.2.sublayer_path": "props.usda"})   # adds row 2

usdchunks show <chunk> lists each row's params.

Each value you set cooks what it affects straight away, so setting several cooks several times. Set them inside chunk.change_block() and they count as one change: what they affect cooks once, when the block ends, with every value in place.

from usd_chunks import chunk

with chunk.change_block():
    lift.get_param("tx").value = 1.0
    lift.get_param("ty").value = 2.0
# lift, and everything after it, cooked once

Blocks can nest. An inner block joins the outermost one.

docs.title: Connect chunks
docs.text:
There are two kinds of wire, the same two the graph draws.

The input port sets the order chunks run in. Pass a chunk's inputs first when you make it. You can pass more than one.

lift = scene.create.transform(box)      # box -> Transform
both = scene.create.merge(a, b)         # a and b -> Merge; b wins
scene.connect(b, c)                     # b -> c, for chunks that already exist

Into a Merge, the last input wins, the same as a chunk chained after the others. Where a and b both author the same prim, b's value is the one you get. scene.connect(x, both) wires one more branch in the same way: x takes slot 0, the strongest, as a wire dropped on the Merge in the graph does. To put it lower, give a slot: scene.connect(x, both, slot=2). scene.get_inputs(both) lists the branches, strongest first.

Which chunks made a prim is what the node graph shows when you select one. Scripts ask with get_chunk_stack, the chunk version of prim.GetPrimStack():

stack = scene.get_chunk_stack("/World/box")   # [lift, box]: strongest first
scene.set_selected_chunks(stack)              # select them in the node graph
scene.get_chunk_prims(lift)                   # the other way: [Sdf.Path("/World/box")]

scene.trace_prim(path) says who did what: .made_by (the chunk that made it), .changed_by (the chunks that changed it, in the order their changes apply) and .via (for a prim inside an asset a chunk brought in: the asset's prim and that chunk).

A param wire makes one param follow another's value. Pass the param as the value:

scene.create.transform(box, primpath_location=box.get_param("prim_path"))
scene.set(lift, primpath_location=box.get_param("prim_path"))
lift.get_param("primpath_location").connect_value(box.get_param("prim_path"))

All three lines do the same thing. Both kinds of wire are saved with the network.

docs.title: Build one chain
docs.text:
In usdview, only the chunks wired into the graph's Output cook, or into the active View while one is active. The rest are switched off. So build your network as one chain: give each chunk the one before it as its input.

ground = scene.create.ground(prim_path="/set/ground")
box = scene.create.cube(ground, prim_path="/set/box")                              # ground -> box
scene.create.transform(box, primpath_location=box.get_param("prim_path"), ty=0.5)  # box -> Transform

A chunk you make without an input starts a new, separate chain. It stays off until the Output or a View points at it. This is on purpose, so you can build a side branch and look at it later.

To end the graph at a chunk, use scene.set_output(). To look at a chunk, use scene.set_view():

lift = scene.create.transform(box, primpath_location=box.get_param("prim_path"), ty=3.0)
scene.set_output(lift)        # the graph now ends at lift, and it cooks
scene.set_view(box)           # look at box for now, in View 2
scene.set_view(lift, view=3)  # and at lift in View 3
Call Does scene.set_output(chunk) What Set Output does in the graph: the Output's wire moves to chunk, no View stays active, and the graph cooks to the Output. A graph with no Output gets one. scene.set_view(chunk) What Set View does: the View's old input is replaced, that View becomes active, and what it reaches cooks. It uses a View already showing chunk, else the first View the graph doesn't have yet, else the active one. scene.set_view(chunk, view=3) The same, in View 3. Views are numbered 2 and 3, as in the graph, since 1 is the Output.

usdchunks run cooks to the Output, and a ChunkGroup delivers its Output, so end a script with scene.set_output(). Use scene.set_view() to look at something along the way.

A script's own Scene.new() has no Output or View, so all its chunks cook, until you call one of these. Build one chain there too: the saved network then works when you open it in usdview.

docs.title: Backdrops and notes
docs.text:
A backdrop frames chunks in the graph, and a sticky note says what part of it is for. See Backdrops and sticky notes.

frame = scene.add_backdrop([box, lift], title="Geometry", color="Green")
note = scene.add_note("Builds the box and lifts it", at=box)

scene.set_backdrop(frame, title="Box", color=(0.6, 0.3, 0.2))
scene.set_backdrop(frame, around=[box, lift, cap])   # fit it around these
scene.chunks_in_backdrop(frame)                      # [box, lift, cap]
scene.get_backdrops()                                # [frame, note]
scene.remove_backdrop(note)                          # the chunks stay
Call Does scene.add_backdrop(chunks, title=, color=) A backdrop around the chunks, in their graph. Or give rect=(x, y, w, h) instead of chunks. scene.add_note(text, at=) A note just above a chunk, or at an (x, y). scene.get_backdrops(context=None, notes=True) The backdrops and notes in a graph. context is a ChunkGroup; None is the graph new chunks go in. scene.set_backdrop(b, title=, color=, rect=, around=) Change any of them. What you leave out stays. scene.chunks_in_backdrop(b) The chunks in it: the ones that move with it in the graph. scene.remove_backdrop(b) Delete it.

A colour is a name (Grey, Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Teal, Blue, Purple) or (r, g, b) from 0 to 1. Graph coordinates have y pointing down, as on screen. Each call returns or takes the backdrop's USD prim (or its prim path). backdrops.read(prim) from usd_chunks.graph gives its title, colour, rect and whether it is a note.

docs.title: with blocks
docs.text:
with chunk: says where the chunks made inside it go.

  • A chunkgroup: they go inside the group.
  • Any other chunk: it becomes their input. Each chunk made inside runs after it, unless you give it inputs of your own.

Use a group to keep chunks together:

props = scene.create.chunkgroup(name="Props")
with props:
    crate = scene.create.cube(prim_path="/props/crate")

Use an Edit Target to write into a layer. The chunks after an Edit Target write into its layer:

shot = scene.create.layer(layer_name="shot")

with scene.create.edit_target(shot, edit_target="shot"):
    ground = scene.create.ground(prim_path="/set/ground")
    scene.create.rect_light(ground, primpath_location="/set/key")

The ground and the light go into the shot layer. A Layer chunk only makes the layer. The Edit Target is what sends edits to it.

docs.title: Department layers side by side
docs.text:
A Layer chunk goes into whatever layer is being edited where it is wired. So a second Layer wired after a chunk inside the first one's Edit Target lands inside the first layer: lighting nested in layout, not beside it. For department layers that sit side by side, end each department with an Edit Target back to Session Layer, and wire the next Layer after that:

world = scene.create.prim(primpath_location="/World", prim_type="Xform")

layout = scene.create.layer(world, layer_name="layout")
into = scene.create.edit_target(layout, edit_target="layout")
box = scene.create.cube(into, prim_path="/World/box")
back = scene.create.edit_target(box, edit_target="Session Layer")   # out of layout

lighting = scene.create.layer(back, layer_name="lighting")
into = scene.create.edit_target(lighting, edit_target="lighting")
key = scene.create.distant_light(into, primpath_location="/World/key", intensity=3.0)
back = scene.create.edit_target(key, edit_target="Session Layer")   # out of lighting

layout and lighting are now both sublayers of the session layer, the box is in layout and the light in lighting. An Export USD chunk after the last back writes each to its own file, layout.usda and lighting.usda.

The session layer is then the shot: the stage settings and the departments as sublayers. export_usd(back, output_dir=".", session_file_name="shot", bake_all=True) writes it as shot.usda, plain USD without the network. examples/scripts/shot_departments.py is a whole shot built this way, on a set file, and runs as written.

docs.title: Save and cook
docs.text: Call Does scene.save(path) Writes the network: Chunk prims and wires. It opens as a graph. scene.export(path) Writes the result as plain USD, without the Chunk prims. scene.execute() Runs every chunk. You rarely need it: chunks cook when they are made and when a value changes. scene.commit() Runs the chunks that write files, such as Export USD.

docs.title: File paths
docs.text:
A file path in a param (a Sublayer's, a Reference's, a texture's) follows USD's rules, with the network file as the file it is written in:

  • inputs/set.usda, with no ./ or ../, is a USD search path. It is found in the network's folder, from whatever directory the network runs in.
  • ../inputs/set.usda is relative to the network file, as it would be in any USD file.
  • An absolute path works only on a machine where that file is, so it logs a warning. Saving writes one that sits under the network's folder relative to it (Stage Settings' Relative File Paths, on by default; scene.save(path, relative_paths=False) turns it off for one save).

A network that isn't saved yet has no folder, so its relative paths are found from the working directory until it is. Give Scene.new the file you will save to, and they are found from that folder from the start:

with Scene.new(path="shots/sh010/shot_network.usda") as scene:
    street = scene.create.reference(file_path="../../sets/street.usda", primpath_location="/set")
    ...
    scene.save()      # to the path given to Scene.new

Saving to another folder keeps each relative path naming the same file. A file that is not found logs a warning naming the folders it was looked for in.

docs.title: Build a big network fast
docs.text:
Each chunk you make cooks what it affects straight away. In a long network that is often the whole chain above it, again and again. Make the chunks inside chunk.change_block() instead:

with chunk.change_block():
    ...  # make and wire hundreds of chunks
# here everything has cooked, once

Inside the block each chunk cooks once as it is made, before it is wired, and nothing else cooks. When the block ends, what changed since then cooks once, upstream first: about two cooks per chunk. A readout you read inside the block is from that first, unwired cook. A 336-chunk network took 250 s this way, against 17-27 minutes.

docs.title: Write the network without cooking it
docs.text:
To only write a network, open the scene lazily. Nothing cooks until you ask for a result:

with Scene(stage, lazy=True) as scene:      # or Scene.open(path, lazy=True)
    stand = scene.create.noise_field(...)   # marked, not cooked
    pines = scene.create.scatter_points(stand, ...)
    sun = scene.create.distant_light(pines, intensity=30.0)
    scene.cook(pines)                       # cooks Stand and Pines, nothing else
    print(pines.get_param("readout").value) # fresh
    scene.save("forest_network.usda")       # writes the network, as it stands
  • scene.cook(chunk) cooks that chunk and what is still marked above it. Do this before you read a result: an OUTPUT param, or prims a chunk wrote. The chunk itself always cooks, even when nothing marked it, so it also picks up what a script changed behind the framework's back (a Scatter Brush's painted field, set as a Python attribute). It works the same in an eager Scene. scene.cook() with no chunk cooks everything.
  • export and commit cook everything first, each chunk once.
  • save writes the network as it stands. It does not cook it.
  • Leaving the block cooks nothing. Closing the scene removes every result anyway.

Some chunks build params in their cook, such as a Light's schema inputs. They take the values you give at create in that first cook, the same way a saved network's values come back when you open it. A save cooks only those chunks, alone, without what is above them, so their values are saved. The catch: a misspelled param name raises at the chunk's first cook, not at create.

The woodland forest network (40 chunks, 8.5M instances) took about 12 minutes to write the old way. Lazily it takes 6 s.

docs.title: Inside usdview
docs.text:
Scene.current() gives you the scene usdview is running. What you make goes into it:

  • The chunks go into the graph you are looking at. If you have gone into a chunkgroup, they go into that group.
  • The first node goes to the middle of the graph view. The next ones go in a row to its right. Each with block starts a new row.
  • Leaving the with block does not close usdview's scene.
  • If the graph has no Output yet, it adds one at the end of your chain.
  • If the graph already has an Output, new chunks start switched off, the same as nodes you make in the graph: they are not in the Output's chain yet. To cook them, call scene.set_output(last) with the chain's last chunk, or scene.set_view(last) to look at it. In the graph, you can instead select that node and press V, which makes a View. Press 2 or 3 to switch between Views, and 1 to go back to the Output.

docs.title: Live sessions
docs.text:
A live session keeps a network open, and you change its params from another terminal or a script. Each change cooks only what it reaches, then commits again, so a Render chunk renders again. Opening the file and the first cook happen once, not on every change.

Start one:

usdchunks run shot.usda --live

It cooks the network as run does, then waits. Ctrl+C ends it. From another terminal:

usdchunks send shot.usda Fill.intensity=8 Sky.intensity=2 --wait
usdchunks send shot.usda --list     # every param you can set, with its type
usdchunks send shot.usda --reset    # clear every value sent so far

--wait returns once the session has cooked the change, and rendered it if the network renders. Without it, send returns as soon as the values are written.

The same from Python, for a script that tries values one after another:

from usd_chunks import live

for strength in (2, 4, 8):
    live.send("shot.usda", {"Fill.intensity": strength}, wait=True)
    ...  # look at the render

Name a param as run takes it: Chunk.param. The last part is enough when only one of the chunk's params ends with it, so Fill.intensity finds the Light's attr_grp.inputs:intensity. When two chunks in different groups share a name, --list shows their params under the prim path instead, such as /chunks/Group/Fill.attr_grp.inputs:intensity, and /chunks/Group/Fill.intensity finds it. A name send cannot find gets the closest matches in the error.

The session and send share two files beside the network:

File Written by Holds shot.live.usda send The values, as USD overs on the Chunk prims. shot.live.json the session Every param it can set, and which change it has finished.

The session holds shot.live.usda as a sublayer of its session layer and reloads it when the file changes. A value arrives as an edit on the stage, the same as one made in the graph. The network file itself is never written.

The values stay in shot.live.usda after the session ends, and the next session opens with them. --reset clears them. To keep them, set them in the network.

While a session runs, the Render chunk keeps its renderer between renders. The renderer builds its scene once and then updates only what a change touched. The renderer's whole scene stays in memory for as long as the session runs.

Two limits:

  • send sets only the params the session lists. A chunk can build some params only when their group is opened (Render Settings does, for each renderer's settings). Such a param is listed once the network has a value for it.
  • A value in shot.live.usda is stronger than a change to the same param in the graph. Clear it with --reset to edit that param in the graph again.

docs.title: Five boxes in a row
docs.text:
from usd_chunks import Scene

with Scene.new() as scene:
    last = scene.create.cube(prim_path="/geo/box0")
    for i in range(1, 5):
        box = scene.create.cube(last, prim_path=f"/geo/box{i}")
        last = scene.create.transform(box, primpath_location=box.get_param("prim_path"), tx=i * 3.0)
    scene.export("boxes.usda")

docs.title: Open a saved network and change it
docs.text:
from usd_chunks import Scene

with Scene.open("box_network.usda") as scene:
    lift = scene.get_chunk("Transform")
    scene.set(lift, ty=10.0)
    scene.export("box_high.usda")

scene.get_chunk(name) finds a chunk by its node name.

docs.title: A light with its values set
docs.text:
from usd_chunks import Scene

with Scene.new() as scene:
    scene.create.rect_light(primpath_location="/set/key", intensity=5.0, exposure=2.0)
    scene.export("light.usda")

docs.title: A small set
docs.text:
Ground, three colored boxes, a sky light and a camera, in one chain:

from usd_chunks import Scene

colors = [(1.0, 0.2, 0.2), (0.2, 1.0, 0.2), (0.2, 0.4, 1.0)]

with Scene.new() as scene:
    last = scene.create.ground(prim_path="/set/ground")
    for i, (r, g, b) in enumerate(colors):
        box = scene.create.cube(last, prim_path=f"/set/box{i}")
        path = box.get_param("prim_path")
        moved = scene.create.transform(box, primpath_location=path, tx=i * 2.0 - 2.0, ty=0.5)
        last = scene.create.set_display_color(moved, prim_path=path, color_r=r, color_g=g, color_b=b)
    sky = scene.create.dome_light(last, primpath_location="/set/sky")
    scene.create.camera(sky, primpath_location="/set/cam", ty=2.0, tz=10.0)

    scene.save("set_network.usda")
    scene.export("set.usda")

More examples are in examples/scripts/.

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text: scene.create is a short way to make chunks. It calls ChunkRegistry().get_chunk_module(name), then the module's create() or load(), then scene.add_chunk(chunk). The loader, paste and the graph use these calls too. Use them directly if you need to make a chunk without adding it to the scene (chunk.create_chunks(name, anonymous=True)). To build a network, use scene.create.

docs.title: Liquid on surfaces: condensation, runs, drips
docs.text:
Water on glass is made from general tools rather than one "condensation" chunk. Each step writes plain USD, and the next one reads it.

Noise Field ──► (Density Field) ──► Scatter Points "RunSeeds" ──► Surface Flow ──► Trails ──► Curves To Mesh
     │                                                                 │              │
     │                                                                 └► Scatter Points "RunHeads" (Painted Points)
     └────────► (Density Field) ──► Scatter Points "Drops"  ◄── Keep Away From ─────┘
Chunk Writes Houdini equivalent Noise Field a 0..1 vertex primvar on meshes. Only GeomSubsets limits it to, say, a bottle's glass and keeps it off the label Attribute Noise Scatter Points instances on a surface. The Density Field makes them cluster. Spacing Follows Scale packs small instances between big ones without overlap. Scale Bias gives many small and few big. Keep Away From keeps them clear of other geometry, such as the runs Scatter + Copy to Points, with a relax on pscale Surface Flow a Points prim over time: each source point crawls over a surface under a force such as gravity, with wander, stop-and-go stickiness and a travel limit a POP network with the particles stuck to the surface Trails one curve per point, through everywhere it has been. Width Variation swells and thins it along its length, and Sink presses it into the surface so a tube reads as a film of water. Grow animates the curves drawing themselves Trail SOP Curves To Mesh a tube along each curve, so the runs render in any delegate Sweep

Why not the RBD Solver for the runs: a rigid body on a wall falls off it, and nothing in a rigid-body solver keeps a drop against glass. Surface Flow's points live on the surface, which is the general version of the idea. The same chunk also covers rain on a window, sap on bark and paint runs.

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• New mesh. Point the model's Reference at it and set the GeomSubsets that should get wet. Every surface path is a parameter, so nothing else changes.
  • New look. Change the seeds: Noise Field for where the clusters are, RunSeeds for where runs start, Surface Flow for their paths, Drops for the drops.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text: C:\UsdScenes\chunk_demos\condensation\condensation_can.usda is a close-up packshot of a soda can, in centimetres. It is built by build_condensation_can.py in the same folder, which also converts the can from OBJ and writes the droplet prototypes and a backdrop as assets. The scene itself is chunks only. The water is a MaterialX standard_surface with transmission. Storm cannot refract, so the material keeps a little base colour to stay visible in the viewport.

docs.title: Undo and redo
docs.text: usd_chunks undoes what chunks author, on any host, in pure Python on the host's own pxr. It does not undo anything else.

docs.title: What is undone
docs.text:
• Chunk prims: every prim the stage says is a Chunk -- its params, wires, view, position and metadata. Adding and deleting chunks, too.
  • Backdrops and sticky notes in a chunk graph: moving, resizing, recolouring, editing their text, adding and deleting them.
  • Wherever they are authored in the stage's own layers: the root layer, the session layer, department sublayers the Edit Target picked, and overs on the prims a Reference chunk brought in.
  • Cooked output is not recorded: it lives in each chunk's own layer, and cooking after an undo makes it again.

docs.title: What is not undone
docs.text:
• Prims that are not chunks: scene data authored directly, edits by other plugins or by scripts writing to the stage.
  • Layers outside the stage's own layer stack, such as a referenced asset file edited in place.
  • Layer-level changes: adding, removing or reordering a sublayer, or layer metadata (defaultPrim, upAxis).
  • Chunk prims nested inside variant sets.

If you need those undone, use the C++ usd-undo plugin, or your host's own USD undo. usd-undo records every field edit on any layer it is attached to; it has to be built against your host's USD.

docs.title: Per host
docs.text:
